entries.title: The talent review list is rated by managers with something to lose
entries.summary: A leader has a role the program can't afford to miss and a talent review list with three names. In one large manufacturer, managers with more to lose from a departure were more likely to rate their people's potential lower than performance suggested. Who rated each name?
entries.operatingMove: For a role that is hard to fill and costly to get wrong, treat the list as leads. Ask for delivered work the current manager did not write. Let someone outside the person's reporting line decide whether the person can move. Help the manager replace the person.
entries.preview: In one company, workers' applications for new jobs rose 78 percent in the quarter their manager moved. This paper shows what that means for a list rated by managers, and how to check yours.
entries.bodyHtml:
Suppose a leader in an enterprise project management office has to fill one role that will decide whether a late program recovers: the lead for the cutover to a new system. Few people in the company have done the job before. The leader opens the talent review list, which names the employees whose managers rate them ready for bigger roles. Three names are on it. The list reads like a neutral record of who is ready. Who rated each name, and what does that manager lose if the person moves?

What one company's records show

Ingrid Haegele studied a large German manufacturer where each manager gives a worker two ratings at the same time. Performance stays inside the team. Potential, the rating for bigger jobs, goes into lists that HR circulates across the company. Managers with more of their pay tied to team results, and managers with smaller teams, were more likely to rate someone's potential lower than performance would predict. Asked how often a leader might need to talk a team member out of exploring another department because of team needs or goals, three-fourths of managers said at least sometimes. Also, 55 percent agreed that developing talent is a conflict of interest, because developed people are more likely to leave.

So the list can already carry a staffing decision. In that firm, the managers with the most to lose when someone left were more likely to rate their people's potential lower than performance suggested, and the potential rating is the one the rest of the company sees.

People also stay out of view by not applying. In the quarter a manager moved to another team, workers' applications for jobs elsewhere in the company rose by 78 percent. The people who applied only because their manager was leaving were hired 49.1 percent of the time. The average applicant was hired 27.6 percent of the time. That is one company, and its measure counts applications to posted jobs. A scarce role filled by appointment skips that step but still starts from the list.

Why pay and ratings are not an easy fix

The leader typically does not set the pay of managers on other teams, and a working paper on manager pay finds that fixing it can cost more than it returns. Fairer ratings face a limit too. In a study of developmental ratings of more than 2,000 managers, each rated by seven people, the raters' own habits explained more than half of the differences in ratings. The person being rated explained about a fifth to a quarter. A calibration meeting puts managers in one room to compare ratings, and it leaves each manager's stake where it was.

A staffing rule for scarce roles

For the few roles that are hard to fill and costly to get wrong, treat the list as leads. Ask for delivered work the current manager did not write, such as results recorded by the program that received it. Let someone outside the person's reporting line decide whether the person can move, once the person says they want the role. Help the manager replace the person, and credit the manager for what the person does next. No study has tested these four steps together. They are a recommendation built from the studies.

What to do next

Take the last three scarce roles you filled from a list. For each, write down who was on the list, who rated each name, and how much of that manager's pay depends on team results. Then ask the programs that received work from people across the company for the last two years of delivered results, and write down anyone with strong results who was not on the list. If that second list is not empty, the list has been missing people for the roles you can least afford to get wrong. The white paper has the six studies, the limits of each, and a made-up case.

entries.title: Average accuracy doesn't tell you what you could lose
entries.summary: Zillow reported a 6.9 percent typical miss across 104 million homes not listed for sale. Its money sat in the homes whose owners said yes. A model's average accuracy does not tell you how it did on the cases you accept.
entries.operatingMove: Treat the cases you accept as their own group. Track the acceptance rate against plan, the error, and the money lost, and raise the cap on what you sign only while all three stay inside limits you set.
entries.preview: The people who say yes to a model's offer can know more than the model does, and your own approval rule hides the cases you turn away. This paper shows how to measure the cases you accept, keep error and loss apart, and cap what you commit.
entries.bodyHtml:
In June 2021, Zillow announced a more accurate home-value model: a 6.9 percent median error, the typical miss, across more than 104 million homes not listed for sale. The release said Zillow's growing confidence in the Zestimate's accuracy had led it to start making live cash offers. Less than five months later, Zillow said it would shut the program down. It had bought 9,680 homes in one quarter and written down the value of the homes it held by $304 million.

Zillow's shareholder letter gives other reasons too: price forecasts that missed by more than it had modeled, and more purchases than its renovation and resale capacity could absorb. It also says a larger share of owners accepted its offers than it had seen before, because it was paying more than it later expected the homes to sell for. The letter never mentions the 6.9 percent. That number covered 104 million homes. Zillow's money sat in the homes whose owners said yes.

The people who say yes are not a random sample

Suppose a model prices used vans $1,000 too high or $1,000 too low, half each, so its average error is zero. A company offers the model's price minus $500 and plans to keep the $500 as its margin. The owners know their vans. Owners of vans priced too high say yes, and the rest say no. The company buys the overpriced half and loses $500 on each van, though the average error never changed.

Two studies look at the same problem. In a simulation of a home buyer in Oslo, expected profit fell from about 6 to 8 percent to about 0 to 1 percent once owners were assumed to accept overpriced offers more readily than underpriced ones. In real purchases by iBuyers, companies that make fast cash offers on homes, profits fell as the companies moved into areas where a standard price model missed more.

Your own approval rule hides errors too. A lender sees how approved loans turn out, but not how refused loans would have turned out. A report built from your own results describes the cases you chose.

Measure the cases you accept

Treat the accepted cases as their own group and track three numbers for it. The acceptance rate against plan is the only one you see before outcomes arrive. Error is how far the estimate was from what happened. Loss is the money actually lost after margin and costs.

Cap what you commit at signing

Outcomes arrive after the commitments, so set the limit when you sign. The leader who would bear the loss sets a cap on the accepted group, in cases or dollars, and writes down the limits for all three numbers before raising it. Raise the cap one step at a time, and lower it or stop when any number leaves its limit. A cap costs growth, so the same leader weighs that against what a bad run could cost.

Ask for the number on the accepted cases

Pick one workflow where a model's estimate sets a commitment that someone else can refuse. Write down who says yes, compare the accepted cases with the declined ones where you can see them, and set the cap and the limits.

Zillow's June release said how accurate the Zestimate was on 104 million homes. It did not say how accurate it was on the homes whose owners said yes. Ask for that number before you sign the next increase. The white paper has the evidence, the sources, and the full method.

entries.title: Why the kill gate doesn't fire
entries.summary: A committee can have the power to stop a failing program and still approve more funding. People who approved it may want to keep it going. For a big program, let someone with no prior approval decide after a missed target.
entries.metaDescription: A kill gate often fails because the continue-or-stop decision goes back to the people who approved the program. Let a reviewer who did not approve it decide.
entries.operatingMove: For a big program, record its minimum result, due date, how the sponsor will be judged, and a reviewer who did not approve it.
entries.preview: A committee can have the power to stop a program and still extend it. Research suggests that people may add money to an earlier choice after it goes badly. For a big or hard-to-reverse program, set at approval the minimum result the program must reach by a due date. Judge sponsors on the case. If the program falls short, a reviewer who did not approve it decides.
entries.bodyHtml:
A program is late and costing more than planned. The sponsor asks for one more quarter. The committee that approved the first funding rounds can stop the work, but it approves the request. A quarter later, the same choice returns.

A tougher gate will not solve that problem by itself. The committee already had the power to stop. The people deciding also helped make the commitment they now have to end.

Studies of escalation show that people who own a losing choice often keep putting resources into it. A review of that research found the pull stronger in four samples where the person deciding was monitored by someone else. Because the pull rose when the responsible person was monitored, a sponsor who recommends in front of a reviewer may lean toward continuing, which is why the sponsor only recommends and the reviewer decides. A funding review puts a sponsor before the committee that approved the same case.

The answer is not to remove the sponsor. The sponsor knows the work. Move only the continue-or-stop decision after a pre-set miss.

First, record the minimum result and its due date. It is the point below which the original case no longer holds. It is not the forecast.

Second, tell the sponsor that the review will judge the quality of the case and how early a miss is raised. Do not judge only the final result.

Third, name a reviewer who had no part in the approval. When the minimum is missed, the sponsor brings the evidence and recommends continue, narrow, pause, or stop. The reviewer decides. The EPMO tracks the date and calls the review.

The reviewer can still continue a program on a revised case. Use this step for large or hard-to-reverse commitments. The evidence comes from laboratory studies, a small shared-authority sample, and related field studies; no study has tested this full design.

At the next funding approval, write the minimum, its date, how the sponsor will be judged, and who decides after a miss. The next request for one more quarter then goes to someone who does not have to reverse an earlier approval.

How prior approval can pull people toward continuing
Three steps: set a minimum, judge the case, and name a reviewer

entries.title: Who owns governance?
entries.summary: In a meeting that crosses domains, every domain signs off on its own area. Nobody in the room owns the enterprise decision itself. A stack of approvals is not a decision — so who owns it?
entries.metaDescription: Every domain signs off on its own area and nobody owns the enterprise decision. Six questions an EPMO answers to turn a stack of approvals into one choice.
entries.operatingMove: For any decision big enough to cross domains, have the EPMO answer six questions before approval. What outcome are we after, and who owns it? Which rules and limits apply? What do we know about conditions now? What options are still open, and what does each cost the portfolio? Who decides, and who can grant an exception? What would reopen the decision?
entries.preview: The sponsor asks whether the program is approved to proceed. Security, data governance, architecture, operations, and finance each give a defensible answer. Together they describe an investment nobody actually chose. This field note shows why a stack of approvals leaves the enterprise decision unmade, and which part of governance the EPMO should own.
entries.bodyHtml:
The sponsor asks one question: "Are we approved to proceed?"

Security says yes, as long as the rollout is more tightly controlled. Data governance says yes, but not using customer transcripts the way the plan assumes. Architecture can support the design once one dependency is cleared. Operations can't run the old and new processes side by side for the whole switchover. Finance points out that all of these changes remove the cheaper option and push the payoff date back.

Every team is right about its own area. Add the answers up, though, and you get an investment nobody actually chose. All those approvals put the decision on the table. None of them made it.

The missing job

Think about driving. The road authority sets the rules. The car has its limits and safety systems. The driver picks the destination and owns the trip. Navigation pulls the destination, the traffic, the closures, and the routes into one view so the driver can choose. It doesn't write the traffic laws, and it doesn't decide where to go. It just makes a responsible choice possible.

That navigation role is the one missing in the meeting, and it's the one the EPMO should own: the framework around a cross-domain choice — what is being decided, which evidence has to be weighed, what options remain, and who has the authority to decide.

Approvals are not a decision

A strategic program can finish every review and still be ungoverned. Each condition attached to a yes can be sound on its own while, together, they add up to a different investment than the one the sponsor asked the organization to approve. Collecting approvals does not make the decision.

In the meeting above, the plan that was approved no longer works under what's now known. The organization could keep the outcome by funding the tighter design, or narrow the outcome to fit the limits. It could change the order, free up capacity elsewhere, wait, or stop. No single function can make that enterprise choice.

The EPMO shouldn't overrule the specialists. It should show the sponsor whether the original outcome still holds and how the remaining options would affect the portfolio. The record also has to say who can decide and what new evidence would force another look.

What the EPMO owns

Enterprise leaders own the strategic and risk limits. Domain leaders own their standards, evidence, and expert judgments. The sponsor owns the outcome. A delegated forum or executive owns the investment decision within its authority. Independent assurance owns its review and challenge.

The EPMO owns the framework that ties the decision together. It keeps track of who owns what and what evidence each domain has to bring. It frames the portfolio options and names who decides and who can grant an exception. It keeps the escalation path, the decision record, and the review triggers. The framework makes sure the authorized decision weighs the right evidence and can be reconstructed later. It doesn't take over the expert judgments or the business outcome.

The framework comes down to six questions. What outcome are we after? Which rules and limits apply? What do we know about current conditions? What options are still open? Who decides, and who can grant an exception? What would reopen the decision? Each one produces something an authorized leader can actually use. Together, they turn separate domain reviews into one enterprise choice without stripping the domains of their authority.

The conversation to have first

When an organization says the EPMO owns governance, start by asking which decisions it means. Assign each standard to its domain owner and the outcome to its sponsor. Name the authority that can accept an exception or change the investment. Then define the evidence that would force another look. Those answers turn a vague assignment into a usable operating model.

The real test is whether a skeptical executive can reconstruct the decision. That executive should be able to see the intended outcome, the limits that applied, and what the experts found. The record should show the options, who decided, the conditions they accepted, and the review trigger. A stack of meetings and status colors can't provide that.

Come back to the sponsor's question. The honest answer isn't a pile of domain approvals. It's the recorded decision an authorized leader made after seeing the conditions and their combined effect on the investment. The framework that makes that decision possible is the part of governance the EPMO owns.

entries.title: Felt productivity is not measured productivity
entries.summary: Ask people how much faster AI made them and they can give you a number. In a careful randomized trial that checked that number against a clock, it ran well ahead of the work. Judge the tool on what it delivered, measured against a baseline, and keep self-reported speed in a record of its own.
entries.metaDescription: In one trial, developers believed AI sped them up while the clock showed the opposite. Judge AI on delivered output against a baseline, not on self-reported speed.
entries.operatingMove: Before scaling an AI-assisted workflow, require three things. First, a baseline, taken before the tool or rebuilt from a held-back group, staged waves, or work records. Second, an output measure that heavier use cannot inflate. Third, a review that keeps felt speed and delivered output in separate columns.
entries.preview: This field note starts with a randomized trial that checked developers’ own estimates of their AI speedup against a clock. It says what the trial shows and what it does not. It covers METR’s later follow-up, which was unreliable, and why Google Cloud’s DORA survey is not a second proof. It sets a three-part standard: a baseline, an output measure that heavier use cannot inflate, and a review with two columns. It says what to do when the tool is already live and no baseline exists. It also answers the objections to measuring.
entries.bodyHtml:
Ask people how much faster AI made them and they can give you a number. That number is an estimate of how the work felt, not a measurement of what it delivered, and the two can be far apart. When a program is funded, scaled, or defended on a self-reported speedup alone, the organization has let a feeling stand in for evidence.

The clearest test is a 2025 randomized controlled trial by the research nonprofit METR. Sixteen experienced open-source developers completed 246 real tasks, with and without AI. Beforehand they expected a 24 percent speedup. Afterward they still believed they had gained 20 percent. The clock said they took 19 percent longer. The trial does not show that AI slows people down. It measured expert developers, on projects they knew well, with early-2025 tools. What it shows is one documented case where capable people were wrong about their own speed and stayed wrong after the work was done. A leader should treat a self-reported speedup as an estimate, and judge the tool on delivered output against a baseline.

METR’s later study, with newer tools, estimated that AI-allowed tasks took less time, with ranges wide enough to include no change. METR calls that estimate unreliable, because developers who did not want to work without AI left the study. It believes developers are likely more sped up now, on very weak evidence. Do not quote the early-2025 figure as a rate. It remains the only trial this paper cites that checked a feeling against a clock, and there the feeling was wrong.

A survey by Google Cloud’s DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) program looks like a second match and is not. In 2024, respondents who used AI more reported higher individual productivity, flow (sustained focus), and satisfaction, while the report’s findings on delivery stability and throughput pointed the other way. Both sides of that split are what respondents answered, so it compares two sets of survey answers, not a feeling against a measurement. A year later, the 2025 report linked AI adoption to higher throughput, with delivery instability still rising.

What the sources support together is narrower than “people overrate AI.” The feeling is not a reliable stand-in for the output, and nobody can say from outside which way it errs in a given workflow. An organization scaling AI on a self-reported speedup alone is scaling on sentiment, with no way to tell whether the sentiment is too high or too low.

What to measure instead

The alternative is ordinary, and it has three parts that work in order. First, capture a baseline before the tool changes the work. Then choose a work-output signal that reflects delivered value, such as cycle time, rework, error rate, or finished units meeting standard, and choose it so that using the tool more cannot move it by itself. Finally, review felt experience and delivered outcome in separate columns. When the columns agree, use can grow. When they diverge, the review has found the case a satisfaction survey would have counted as a win.

The tool may already be live by the time anyone asks for a baseline. There are three ways to get a comparison, listed in this paper’s judgment from strongest to weakest: keep a comparable group on the old way for a set period, switch the tool on in waves and compare the waves, or rebuild the before-picture from work records and call it an estimate. If none is possible, the output column reads “not measured.” That is different from a weak result, and expansion waits unless the organization would accept it on the assumption that the gain is zero.

The hard part is deciding which numbers do not count. Adoption rate, active users, prompts per employee, and self-rated speed can all rise while the work stays the same. They belong on an adoption dashboard, not in the evidence a portfolio uses to deepen use. A contributed opinion column in CIO magazine makes the distinction plainly: governance machinery can sit above the work, while the value is created or lost inside the workflow.

Objections, and what measuring costs

The standard has real objections. People can work to an output number, so choose finished units that met the quality bar and read a sample of the work itself. Measuring costs time, and no source prices it, so apply the standard where spending is large or a decision to scale is near. A log of who uses the tool is not a measure of what it delivered, and tracking individuals carries a surveillance cost. Results also age, because the tools change, so measure again at the next decision to expand.

None of this slows adoption. It lets a leader say yes to deeper use on evidence, and redirect rather than abandon a tool whose value is leaking inside a workflow. Felt productivity is real and worth having. It is simply not the same thing as measured productivity, and only one of the two can tell a portfolio where its money went.

entries.title: Separate the decision from the outcome
entries.summary: A green target does not prove a good full outcome or a sound approval. Review the outcome, the route, and the first decision separately.
entries.metaDescription: Hitting the funded target does not prove the decision was sound. How to grade decision quality and the full outcome separately in a portfolio review.
entries.operatingMove: At the next review, first grade the decision from its approval record. Then score the full outcome and compare the route taken with the approved route.
entries.preview: A good result can follow a weak decision. A bad result can follow a sound one. This paper shows leaders how to review the outcome, the route, and the approval without confusing them.
entries.bodyHtml:
A program can hit its benefit target while bypassing controls, exhausting a key team, shifting risk, or harming customers. One green target does not describe everything the program caused.

Reviews can also make the opposite mistake. A program can miss a target after an outside event no one could reasonably predict. A bad result does not prove the approval was poor.

Ask whether the original decision was sound based only on approval-time evidence, what was achieved when the full consequence is counted, and how it was achieved compared with the approved route.

Use two grades and one attribution record. Grade the approval from its original evidence before seeing the outcome score. Then score the full outcome and compare the approved route with the route the team took.

Keep a short record at approval: the problem, alternatives, assumptions, risks, ranges, decision owner, and evidence that would reopen the choice. Keep later facts in a separate column at review.

At the next stage gate, require the record. At the next review, grade the original decision before opening the outcome score. Then score the full outcome and compare the route taken.

entries.title: Capital reallocation is the real portfolio decision
entries.summary: In a study of 1,616 companies, the capital each business unit received in one year closely tracked the year before. A short review run by one owner, with a written trigger and common evidence, can end in a move or a recorded hold.
entries.metaDescription: A short review lets one owner move scarce money and people when evidence changes, or record why to hold, with guards against moving too often.
entries.operatingMove: Choose one scarce resource shared by two initiatives. Write a one-page charter for it, run one review before the next planning cycle, and end with a move or a recorded hold.
entries.preview: An annual plan can keep money and people tied to an old view of the work. This paper describes a short review with a published trigger, common evidence, one decision owner, and a recorded move or hold. A decision horizon keeps a weak reading from setting off a move, and the review counts the cost of moving people and answers the main objections.

Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, Portfolio Management: Fundamental for New Product Success, Stage-Gate International — Cooper and Edgett define portfolio management as a dynamic decision process in which active projects may be sped up, stopped, or deprioritized and resources reallocated, and describe all-project portfolio reviews about four times a year for fast-paced firms; it is a practitioner account.

Alexis Krivkovich, Damian Klingler, Dana Maor, Patrick Guggenberger, and Michael Anzenhofer, The State of Organizations 2026: Three Tectonic Forces That Are Reshaping Organizations, McKinsey & Company, February 19, 2026 — McKinsey reports review cadence, enterprise-wide reallocation, and obstacles named by survey respondents, and says reallocation helps organizations keep up with faster industry cycles; the figures are self-reported and the paper does not treat them as causal proof.

Stephen Hall, Dan Lovallo, and Reinier Musters, How to Put Your Money Where Your Strategy Is, McKinsey & Company, March 1, 2012 — McKinsey's study of 1,616 US-listed companies measures capital received by business units: year-to-year correlation of 0.92, higher returns for top reallocators as an association, and lower returns for heavy reallocators over periods under three years, which the authors suggest is a lag. It does not test initiatives.

U.S. General Accounting Office (now Government Accountability Office), Information Technology Investment Management: A Framework for Assessing and Improving Process Maturity, GAO-04-394G, March 2004 — GAO's 2004 framework for federal technology investments describes portfolio reviews at agreed intervals that compare actual with expected results against predetermined thresholds and adjust resources.

Bent Flyvbjerg, Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View, 2013 — Flyvbjerg reports that front-end cost and benefit estimates typically differ significantly from actual results and proposes checking them against similar completed projects; his evidence comes mostly from large infrastructure projects.

Association for Project Management, What is portfolio management?, APM Body of Knowledge, 8th edition — APM defines portfolio management around strategy and capacity and notes that project sponsors may be required to sacrifice their project priorities for the wider portfolio.
entries.bodyHtml:
In portfolios I have governed under a fixed funding ceiling, leaders tended to treat the annual plan as the decision. The effort went into dividing money and people across initiatives, and the split was then defended until the next planning round. That is an observation from practice, not a measured finding.

The decision that tests whether a portfolio is governed comes later. New evidence shows that one initiative is working, another is not, and a third now matters more. Someone must decide whether to move scarce money and people or leave them where last year's case put them. This paper calls that capital reallocation. It argues that a portfolio unable to make this decision between budget cycles is carrying out last year's plan, not governing. It does not claim that this decision matters more than choosing what to fund.

Quarterly reviews are not new. PMI's portfolio standard and Cooper and Edgett's Stage-Gate guidance both expect periodic reviews that can reallocate resources. Neither gives rules for what such a review can decide. In McKinsey's 2026 survey of more than 10,000 leaders and managers, 47 percent said their organizations review budget and talent only once a year or less. Only 30 percent said their organizations reallocate resources across the whole organization. The answers are self-reported and describe whole organizations, not single portfolios.

Stephen Hall, Dan Lovallo, and Reinier Musters studied 1,616 US-listed companies from 1990 to 2005. The capital spending each business unit received correlated 0.92, on average, with what it received the year before. Companies in the top third for moving capital averaged annual shareholder returns about 30 percent higher than those in the bottom third. That is an association. Over periods shorter than three years, the companies that moved more earned lower returns. The authors suggest a lag before results become visible.

The study covers business units, not initiatives. Applying it to a portfolio's initiatives is this paper's inference. The figures show that stickiness is normal and that the payoff from moving may take years to show. They do not promise a return.

Survey respondents named resistance and managerial protectionism, slow decision-making, and unwillingness to make bold calls. The study's authors add anchoring on last year's allocation and politics. This paper adds two causes from its own reasoning. Money already spent may be treated as a reason to spend more. Business cases written to win approval may leave a later review little to test. Some staying put is sound, and moving people has a switching cost that is often not written down.

The fix is a standing review that decides whether a contested resource should move. Four controls make it work. A trigger is published in advance. Every initiative brings the same small evidence set. One owner can move money and people across initiatives. Each review ends in a move or a written reason to hold. What these controls change is what the review can decide.

Two settings keep the review from becoming churn. Each initiative gets a decision horizon, the earliest date its evidence can fairly be judged. A move must also hold across two reviews and be worth more than the cost of moving, including the ramp-up time of the people who move. The paper states these as its own reasoning, since no study sets the right horizon.

A single owner concentrates power. The owner should not sponsor a competing initiative, and the record of each move or hold stays open to the people affected. Some money and people are locked by contract, law, or commitments already made, and the charter lists them. The review costs time, so it starts with one contested resource and replaces a status meeting instead of adding one.

A one-page charter holds the rules: what can move and how often the review meets, the trigger, the evidence, the owner, the move-or-hold record, and the decision horizon. Choose one scarce resource shared by two initiatives, write the charter for it, and run one review before the next planning cycle.

The annual plan tells leaders what they believed at the start. Reallocation shows what they do when the evidence changes.

entries.title: Choose AI limits before the model
entries.summary: Before comparing AI vendors, write down the permitted use, the data allowed, the strongest action the tool may take, who owns each part of the work, and what sends the decision back for review. Then choose a model that fits.
entries.metaDescription: Set limits on what the AI may do and touch, before you compare vendors. Then check the vendor you picked against them before you commit.
entries.operatingMove: Take one AI request entering sourcing. Write its five limits on one page before comparing vendors.
entries.preview: A strong demo can make a vendor choice feel settled before anyone agrees on the approved use, data access, or action limit. Set those limits first, test the chosen option before commitment, and reopen the decision if they expand.
entries.bodyHtml:
A model can look impressive and still be wrong for the work, data, or actions an organization is ready to support. Before comparing vendors, state what the tool may do and what it may not do.

Start with five choices: the use, data, action limit, work split, and approval triggers. Name the owner for each. Then compare models that fit those choices.

Set the first limits before the shortlist. Before commitment, test the selected model, hosting, contract, supplier chain, and workflow against them. If the candidate needs broader data or more power, return that change for a visible decision.

This is not legal advice. It gives legal, security, data, procurement, and business owners a reliable set of facts before a vendor's defaults become the operating design.

Record the evidence, owner, date, and status for each choice. Mark it as a fact, judgment, or open question. Give every open question an owner and a due date.

New users, a new region, a different data class, an outside integration, or an automated action can all send the decision back for review.

Use one page for an AI request entering sourcing. Write the use, data, action limit, work split, and review triggers before comparing vendors.

entries.title: Who gets to decide
entries.summary: Evidence does not change work by itself. For choices that matter, name who builds the case, flags a legal, safety, or policy limit that blocks an option, decides, and changes the work.
entries.metaDescription: Name who recommends, who agrees, who decides, and who does the work. Then put those names where the work actually moves.
entries.operatingMove: Pick five recent decisions. Name who built the case, could block an option for a stated reason, decided, and changed the work.
entries.preview: A team can have the right data and still leave with no decision. This paper shows how to name who builds the case, checks for a legal, safety, or policy limit that blocks an option, decides, and makes the change so evidence leads to action.
entries.bodyHtml:
A review can show that a project is late, a risk has changed, or another team needs the same people. The meeting can still end with a request for more analysis when no one has the right to redirect, pause, or stop the work.

An org chart does not answer that question. It names jobs. A decision contract names who takes each step when a real choice arrives.

First, name the recommender. That person builds the case, options, evidence, and due date. Second, name any agree role. Use a veto only for a real legal, safety, or policy limit, and require an option or an escalation path.

Third, name the decider. One person can close most operating choices. A board or required group can decide when the rules demand it, but the contract must say how the group closes the vote. Fourth, name the performer who changes the funding, work, permission, or record.

Add the four jobs to the intake form, stage gate, decision record, and delivery tool. If an agree role rejects a plan, record the limit, an acceptable option, and where the case goes next. If the decider misses the due date, pause, escalate, or use a short, recorded extension.

An agent can prepare a recommendation or act inside an approved limit. Named people still set the limit, decide exceptions, and own recovery. A rule can stop an unsafe action without gaining the right to restart the work.

Use the full contract for choices that are hard to reverse, affect other teams, or create real exposure. Keep low-cost choices close to the work.

Pick five recent decisions. Trace who built the case, who could block it, who closed it, and who changed the work. Repair the missing role, rule, or workflow step before the next decision arrives.

entries.title: Standardize the component, not the project
entries.summary: A project folder can preserve files without helping the next team. Share the small part of the work that another team has used, and name who will keep it current.
entries.metaDescription: Do not turn a whole project into a template. Promote the smallest piece that travels, once another team has used it and someone owns it.
entries.operatingMove: Review one repeated check or handoff rule. Ask where another team used it, what may change, who owns it, and when to retire it.
entries.preview: Suppose another team copies a successful project's files, edits them, and saves a new version. Soon nobody knows which rule to follow. The EPMO can help the right owners decide what part of the work has earned reuse.

Smith, and Shawn Wray, AI Adoption Maturity Model v1.0, Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute, June 30, 2026 — SEI describes repeatable results and ongoing improvement.

entries.bodyHtml:
In one release portfolio I supported, teams reached testing with different scopes, schedules, and test needs. Yet each handoff needed an answer to the same readiness question. A full project plan could not move from team to team unchanged.

Consider what can happen when a project ends. The files go into a shared folder. Another team copies them, changes what does not fit, and saves a new version. Soon there are several files with similar names, different rules, and no clear owner. The files survived. The lesson did not.

Rowe and Sikes's PMI paper says teams need to study lessons and act on them, not just store them. GAO found the same gap at NASA. The agency had a lessons system, but GAO found no assurance that later missions used what earlier teams had learned. A folder helps people find a file. It cannot decide which part of the work others should use.

The EPMO can help make that choice. It can find the small part of the work that teams can share, name where local choice still matters, and make sure an owner keeps it current.

Whole projects are hard to share. Sponsors, contracts, risks, and teams differ. Copying a full project brings those local choices with it. The next team must then follow a large template or quietly tear it apart.

Share a smaller part instead: an intake question, a decision record, a readiness check, or a handoff rule. Each has one job. Another team can test it without copying the whole project.

Say what must stay the same and what the next team may change. For a decision record, the decider and evidence may be required; a team may add fields for its own risks. Kirchmer's APQC report supports shared rules with valid local forms. The owner must keep both the common rule and its approved forms clear.

A useful file should not become a standard because one leader likes it or one project went well. Another team must show that it can use the same part. I call the five states iterate, mature, canonize, lock, and monitor. These names mark choices about how much teams may depend on a component, not an industry scale or a promise of return.

Iterate means the first team can still change the idea quickly. Mature means another team tests what can travel. At canonize, the right owners approve the shared rule, its limits, and valid local forms. Lock gives changes a visible path. Monitor means the owner watches for workarounds, stale rules, and reasons to retire it.

Keep the review short enough to make a choice at the table. Ask seven questions:

What exact part of the work has appeared in more than one project?

Where did another team use it, and what changed in the work?

Who owns the rule and can approve, change, or retire it?

What must stay the same, and what may teams change?

How will people find the current version and ask for a change?

Which repeated workaround or failure will force a review?

What would show that the rule is no longer worth keeping?

Do not count downloads as proof. A team may attach the standard decision record, then make the real choice in a side meeting. Look for use at the point where the rule was meant to help.

Valid local differences belong in the shared rule. PMI-sponsored innovation-governance research on six large organizations found a need for both firm rules and room to adapt. The practical step is to label each change so others know what it means.

An approved variant is a local form that repeats under a named circumstance while keeping the rule's purpose. A one-time exception needs an owner and an end point. A change to the shared core needs proof that the old rule no longer fits. Publish variants, watch exceptions that repeat, and send proposed core changes to the owner. Calling all three “local choice” hides what the organization needs to learn.

The EPMO guides the choice to share a rule. It does not write every rule or take every local choice away from the project. Experts keep control of the content. Project leads judge fit. Risk, finance, and other teams keep their own authority.

The EPMO can spot the same problem across projects and bring the right owners together. It can keep approved local forms and current versions visible. It should also let many useful local practices stay local. A shared rule takes real work to maintain.

Another team should be able to find the current rule, know what may change, reach its owner, and report when it fails. That is how project learning becomes useful to others without making every project look the same.

entries.title: The exception path is the real automated workflow
entries.summary: Ask a team that calls its workflow automated to show you the exception queue. It can turn out to be a shared mailbox where everything the automation could not handle quietly piles up. No owners, no classification, no record of what was tried.
entries.metaDescription: A workflow is only automated if it handles the mess. Sort the exceptions, give each kind an owner, and design the way back to normal.
entries.operatingMove: Design the exception path before you call the main path automated. Every kind of exception needs to be detected, routed to a named owner, contained, and brought back to a known state.
entries.preview: The easy path is the simplest part of a workflow to automate. It is also the least useful test of whether the operation is ready. This paper is about what happens when inputs are missing, a case is ambiguous, a dependency changes, or something falls outside what the automation can handle. Moving the routine cases to a machine means the ones left for people tend to be the hard ones. The paper treats the exception path as part of the automated workflow itself: classification, detection and containment, routing, ownership, recovery, and learning. It also says where its evidence stops, how to test the idea on your own workflow, and what that costs.
inside: Why the cases left for people tend to be the hardest ones
How to sort exceptions so each kind has a way to be spotted and an owner
What it takes to get a stuck case back to a known state, and to learn from it

Sculley, Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015) — Sculley and colleagues describe the ongoing maintenance costs of machine-learning systems as data and the outside world shift; the link to a rising exception stream is the paper's own inference.
entries.bodyHtml:
When a team tells me their workflow is automated, I ask to see the exception queue. The answer shows whether anyone owns the cases the automation leaves behind.

What I have seen behind that request is a companion inbox, such as a shared mailbox, where everything the automation could not handle quietly piles up. No classification, no owners, no service expectation. The automation handles its routine volume well. The operation's actual risk, cost, and reputation live in the rest. That is what I observed, not a measured rate. No source in the paper counts how common an unowned exception queue is, so treat the request as a test to run on your own workflow.

There is a reason to expect the cases left over to be the hard ones, and it is the paper's reasoning, not a measured result. Automation is built for the cases that can be recognized and handled by rule or by model, and teams usually automate the easiest first. The cases left with people tend to be the ones it could not handle: the ambiguous, the malformed, the conflicting, the novel, and the unsafe. Lisanne Bainbridge made a related point about industrial control rooms in 1983, so carrying it to business work is an analogy.

The paper's position is that a workflow should not be called automated until its exception path, meaning what happens to every case the automation cannot handle, exists, has owners, and has been rehearsed. The happy path, the cases that run straight through, is the optimization. The exception path has six parts, in operating order, and each depends on the one before.

Classify exceptions

Replace the manual-review bucket with a named list of why processing stopped: bad data, low confidence, policy conflict, failed dependency, suspected harm, novel case. Each class implies a different urgency, skill, and fix.

Detect and contain

The automation must know when it is out of its depth, and stop moving. The failure this prevents is the plausible guess, which turns detectable exceptions into undetected errors.

Route with context

Deliver a decision package, not an alarm: what came in, what was attempted, why it stopped, who is affected, and the clock. Rebuilding context adds nothing to the decision, and the automation already had it.

Assign response ownership

Two owners, not one. Someone resolves this case. Someone else fixes the cause that keeps producing cases like it. Without the second owner, the queue becomes a permanent institution.

Recover to a known state

Resolved means the world is restored: every touched application corrected, partial actions unwound, customers repaired. A case fixed in one application and left wrong in two others is deferred, with interest.

Learn and redesign

Read the queue quarterly as the improvement budget. Measure causes retired, not volume suppressed. A class that vanished because the threshold moved is a risk transfer, not a win.

For a live workflow, start with the queue you already have: open it, classify a sample, and triage by severity before designing anything. A first sort can turn up items that could not wait, such as an aged compliance notice. If exceptions are scattered across email and chat, build the sample from complaints, reversals, and the cases the people who fix them remember. As a planning estimate, a first sort takes a few working days for the workflow owner and the people who work the queue.

Then make the standard binding: a workflow is automated when its exception path is designed, staffed, measured, and rehearsed. Not when its happy path demonstrates throughput. A team that cannot show the taxonomy, the containment test, the context package, the owners, and the rehearsed recovery has a demo with an inbox.

The white paper works through all six parts with their typical failures, the readiness review, the objections and limits, including what the evidence does not show, the build sequence for live workflows, and what the work costs.

entries.title: The coordination tax
entries.summary: A team's drafting tool made one task much faster, and the department's total output did not move. Tracing real cases showed that some of the time had moved into the work around the tool, such as approvals, corrections, and handoffs that no business case counted. No source shows how often this happens, so the paper offers a test: trace one workflow before counting automation savings.
entries.metaDescription: A faster task can leave the workflow no faster. Trace the handoffs, approvals, and exceptions around an automated task before counting the savings.
entries.operatingMove: Before you count an automation's savings, pick one workflow and trace about a dozen recent cases from request to delivery as a starting sample. Sort every handoff, wait, and check by what it produces, price the added work at the seniority of the people who do it, and count the staff time actually freed only after the whole path confirms it.
entries.preview: A task can get much faster while the work around it stays the same size or grows. This paper sets out a six-part review of one workflow, run before a decision to scale. First trace real cases and sort each handoff, wait, and check by what it produces. Then look in three places, in any order: the work around the tool, the handoffs that remain, and the cases the tool cannot handle. Last, measure the whole path. It also covers how to choose the workflow, what the review costs, and where the evidence is thin.
inside: A six-part review that traces where an automated task's saved time may have gone, and the order to run it in
How to sort each handoff and check into four bins, from worth keeping to created by the change
How to choose the workflow, what the review costs, and how much the evidence shows
sourcesHtml: Thomas W. Malone and Kevin Crowston, "The Interdisciplinary Study of Coordination," ACM Computing Surveys 26, no. 1 (1994): 87–119 — Malone and Crowston's 1994 survey defines coordination as managing dependencies among activities and describes kinds of dependency, including shared resources and the link between a producer and a consumer. It is a survey of theory, not a measurement of automation.

Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard, "Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation Under Generative AI," NBER Working Paper 33777 (May 2025, revised March 2026; first circulated as "Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects") — A Danish study that links a late-2024 survey of about 25,000 workers in 11 occupations to administrative records. Users reported time savings of about 3 percent of work hours, and about 8 percent reported entirely new tasks created by chatbots. The answers are self-reported, cover chatbots, and the study finds no sizeable effect on earnings or recorded hours.

Rob Cross, Reb Rebele, and Adam Grant, "Collaborative Overload," Harvard Business Review, January–February 2016 — Cross, Rebele, and Grant report from their own two decades of organizational data that time spent collaborating has grown by 50 percent or more and takes about 80 percent of people's time at many companies. It measures collaboration time in general, not the cost automation creates.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock, and Chad Syverson, "The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies," NBER Working Paper 25148 (2018); published in American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 13(1), 2021 — Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson show that measured productivity can lag when firms invest in unmeasured complements to a general-purpose technology. The evidence is at the level of firms and economies, so the paper uses it as an analogy.

D. Sculley, Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015) — Sculley and colleagues describe how machine-learning systems that are cheap to build become costly to maintain. It is an engineering analysis of one kind of software, used here as an analogy.

Chintan Amrit, Jos van Hillegersberg, and Kuldeep Kumar, "Identifying Coordination Problems in Software Development: Finding Mismatches between Software and Project Team Structures," 2012 — Amrit and colleagues mined code and communication records in a corporate environment and found clashes between software structure and team structure in many projects. A software case study, used here as an analogy.

Harang Ju, "When Coordination Is Avoidable: A Monotonicity Analysis of Organizational Tasks," 2026 preprint — A 2026 preprint that proposes a test for when coordination is required for correctness and applies it to 65 standard workflows and 13,417 job tasks using its own breakdowns. It is not peer reviewed, and the paper treats it as a hypothesis.
entries.bodyHtml:
Automation can cut the effort a task takes and still leave the work around the task untouched. It can even add to that work. Someone still has to route the job, reconcile the numbers, approve the output, explain it, and fix what breaks. The claim here is narrow. When a business case counts only the time saved on the task, the saving it reports can be real while the department keeps less of it, because some of the time moves into the work around the task. This paper does not say that happens in every workflow, and its sources do not say how often it does. It offers a way to find out for one workflow.

One review I carried out makes the problem concrete. A team's drafting tool had made one task much faster, and the team was proud of it. The department's total output had not moved. Tracing real cases from request to delivery showed that some of the time had moved into work around the tool, including an approval step that existed only because the output was now machine-drafted. This paper calls that surrounding work the coordination tax: the work between the tasks, such as routing, waiting, approval, reconciliation, explanation, and repair. A task-level business case often has no line for it, because it is spread across many roles and owned by no one.

The evidence is partial. Researchers define coordination as managing the dependencies among activities, which names this work. A Danish survey of about 25,000 workers found that some chatbot users reported new tasks, such as checking the tool's output, and users reported saving about 3 percent of their work hours. That shows new work can follow adoption. It does not show that the new work cancels a saving in any one workflow. The economists' productivity J-curve and two software studies are analogies, and a 2026 preprint on avoidable coordination is a hypothesis. The paper's claim is a test, not a forecast.

The test is a review of one workflow, run before a decision to scale. Tracing work across a process is not new, since Lean value-stream mapping and process mining both do it. What this paper adds is using the trace to test an automation's business case. The six disciplines have an order. First, trace real cases, not the process diagram, and sort each handoff, wait, and approval along the way by what it produces: worth keeping, reducible, avoidable, or created by the change itself. Next, look in three places, in any order: the work around the tool, the handoffs that remain, and the cases the tool cannot handle. The fourth group, work created by the change, is filled in from what those three find. Last, measure the whole path against the traced baseline, because that is what shows whether the changes worked.

Run the first review on a workflow that already has an automation proposed or recently shipped: about a dozen traced cases as a starting sample, a few observation sessions, and one wall of mapped journeys. As a planning estimate, that is about two weeks of part-time effort. Price the added work at the seniority of the people who do it, and count freed capacity, the staff time the automation actually releases, only after the whole path confirms it. A flat path under a celebrated task measure is a reason to trace, not proof that coordination ate the savings, because demand, staffing, or the mix of cases may also have changed.

The white paper adds how to choose the workflow and what to do when cases cannot be traced, the four-bin sort with a worked example, the handoff contract (a short agreement on what is passed, how the next team accepts it, and who owns each side), the sibling paper The Exception Path Is the Real Automated Workflow for the cases the tool cannot handle, the objections, and the limits of the evidence.

entries.title: An AI evaluation is a production operating control
entries.summary: A workflow can pass its launch evaluation even as the model and cases soon change around it. The vendor updates the model, another team changes inputs, and the business adds new case types. The old result cannot show whether the team can still depend on it, so the workflow owner needs a current test and authority to limit use.
entries.metaDescription: A launch test cannot protect a workflow whose model, inputs, and cases keep changing. Run AI evaluation as a continuing production control instead.
entries.operatingMove: Compare the date of the last production evaluation with the last material change to the model, data, or workflow. If the change came later, retest affected cases or limit use until the evidence catches up.
entries.preview: A launch test describes one version of the system and one set of cases. A production evaluation keeps checking real work as it changes, turning failures into new cases and sending warnings to a named owner who can limit, pause, or restore use.
inside: Why a passing launch test can grow old as models, data, and cases change
How to test real cases and set passing limits before seeing results
Who can limit, pause, or restore use when the evidence changes
sourcesHtml: Chloe Autio, Reva Schwartz, Jesse Dunietz, Shomik Jain, Martin Stanley, Elham Tabassi, Patrick Hall, and Kamie Roberts, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024 — NIST describes ongoing measurement across the generative AI life cycle.

Blake Bullwinkel, Amanda Minnich, Shiven Chawla, Gary Lopez, Martin Pouliot, Whitney Maxwell, Joris de Gruyter, Katherine Pratt, Saphir Qi, Nina Chikanov, Roman Lutz, Raja Sekhar Rao Dheekonda, Bolor-Erdene Jagdagdorj, Eugenia Kim, Justin Song, Keegan Hines, Daniel Jones, Giorgio Severi, Richard Lundeen, Sam Vaughan, Victoria Westerhoff, Pete Bryan, Ram Shankar Siva Kumar, Yonatan Zunger, Chang Kawaguchi, and Mark Russinovich, "Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products," Microsoft Research, January 2025 — Microsoft Research distinguishes red teaming from safety benchmarking.

D. Sculley, Gary Holt, Daniel Golovin, et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28 (NeurIPS 2015) — Sculley and colleagues describe hidden upkeep costs in machine learning systems.
Ziwei Ji, Nayeon Lee, Rita Frieske, et al., "Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation," ACM Computing Surveys, 2023 — Ji and colleagues review errors in fluent generated text.

Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey, "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration," Human Factors 52, no. 3 (2010): 381–410 — Parasuraman and Manzey examine missed automation failures and human bias.
entries.bodyHtml:
Consider a workflow that passes a careful launch test, then falls behind the work it was built to handle. Later, the vendor updates its model, another team changes the input format, and the business adds a case type the test never covered. Each change seems reasonable alone. If no one checks the combined effect, poor results may go unnoticed until a complaint reaches the team.

The launch test was sound, but its result grew old as the system and the work changed. A production evaluation must keep checking today's cases and give the workflow owner power to limit use when the evidence no longer fits.

A benchmark compares models on common tasks, while a red team searches for ways to make one fail. A production evaluation asks whether this team can depend on this system for its current cases. Each result covers only what its test checked, so the team should not use one test to answer another question.

Seven jobs keep that answer current. Choose cases, set limits, keep the tests distinct, watch live work, retest after change, learn from failures, and give someone authority to act.

Build true-to-life cases

Choose cases from real work, including messy inputs and rare errors that would cost the team dearly. Record where those cases came from, then limit use to the kinds of work they represent.

Set thresholds by consequence

A high average can hide failure in a critical case type, so set a limit for each type before testing. Make the limit stricter where an error costs more or where a person must review the answer.

Monitor production signals

Watch for new inputs, more human corrections, rising exceptions, and reviewers who disagree about the same cases. Give each warning a clear trigger and an owner who must respond when it fires.

Turn change into a test event

A model update, prompt edit, or new data source may change answers the team once trusted. Retest the cases that change could affect before people depend on the new version.

Learn from incidents and near misses

After a failure or near miss, look for its cause across the model, data, instructions, and review process. Add a case that would catch it next time, then check whether the fix holds.

Assign authority to change allowed use

Name the workflow owner who can limit, pause, or restore use as the evidence changes. A warning becomes a control only when it reaches someone with the power to decide.

Run it as one system

Cases give the limits meaning; live warnings and system changes tell the team when to retest. Incidents improve the cases, and the owner uses those results to decide how much the workflow may depend on the system.

A passing result supports only the kinds of cases and circumstances the evaluation actually covered. It cannot promise that the system will be safe in every future setting, and it should never approve new case types by analogy. When a model version, source, or workflow changes, the owner must decide whether the existing cases still represent the work and whether allowed use must narrow while the team retests.

The cost of this care should match the stakes. A low-impact workflow may need a modest sample and periodic review, while a workflow people depend on every day needs more frequent checks and a practiced way to stop.

Compare the date of the last production test with the last material change to the model, data, or workflow. If the change is newer, ask what that old test still covers, then retest or limit use until the evidence catches up.

Build the next test from real work, set limits before seeing results, and give each live warning an owner. Fund the time to keep those checks current. The white paper shows how the seven jobs connect and how to match the effort to the risk.

entries.title: Where should this AI run?
entries.summary: A claims tool and a writing aid can need different answers. Compare local, cloud, and hybrid options against each workflow's data, access, actions, support, and exit needs.
entries.metaDescription: Local or cloud AI is a governance decision, not a technology preference. Answer seven questions about the workflow before you name a model.
entries.operatingMove: Run seven checks on two real workflows. Have the workflow owner recommend an option and name who can approve it and accept the remaining risk.
entries.preview: A claims team has two offers: a local model for sensitive records and a cloud service with stronger support. Neither offer yet says who may read the records, what AI may do, or who restores service when it fails. Seven checks turn that gap into a choice a named leader can make.

How two workflows lead to different hosting choices
Who recommends, approves, and accepts the remaining risk

Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, United States Digital Service, and Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program, "Cloud Security Technical Reference Architecture," Version 2.0, June 2022 — CISA's cloud architecture describes shared responsibilities that vary by the service used.
Peter Mell and Timothy Grance, "The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing," NIST Special Publication 800-145, September 2011 — NIST defines cloud computing through service and deployment models.

Wayne Jansen and Timothy Grance, "Guidelines on Security and Privacy in Public Cloud Computing," NIST Special Publication 800-144, December 2011 — NIST's public-cloud guidance explains security and privacy considerations.

Lee Badger, Tim Grance, Robert Patt-Corner, and Jeff Voas, "Cloud Computing Synopsis and Recommendations," NIST Special Publication 800-146, May 2012 — NIST's cloud synopsis discusses cloud computing choices and recommendations.
entries.bodyHtml:
A claims team wants AI to help with sensitive records. One group favors a local model. Another offers a cloud service with stronger support. The leader cannot choose from model quality alone: neither offer yet says who may read the records, what AI may do, or who restores service when it fails.

A low-risk writing aid may need a different answer. Local, cloud, and hybrid are ways to run AI. Each has to meet the needs of the work it supports.

Check data, access, actions, changes, failures, operations, and supplier exit for each workflow. Have the workflow owner recommend an option. A leader with approval authority makes the choice, accepts the remaining risk within that authority, and records when the choice must be reviewed again.

entries.title: The demo-to-production gap
entries.summary: AI has made demos cheap to build, so more of them reach a funding decision with less checking. A demo shows what an AI tool can do with inputs someone chose in advance. Real work asks whether the business can depend on it day to day, as things change, and when something goes wrong.
entries.metaDescription: A demo proves what can work with hand-picked inputs. Real use needs an owner, tested hard cases, a plan for failures, and a way to shut the tool off.
entries.operatingMove: Before real work depends on an AI tool that has only passed a demo, name who owns it, test it on the hard cases, set up monitoring and a recovery plan, and agree in advance who can shut it off and how.
entries.preview: The demo runs clean: a handful of cases picked from thousands, with none of the messy ones that make up much of the real work. Nothing dishonest happens in that room. Demos exist to show what is possible. The failure comes afterward, when a good demo is treated as proof the tool will work in daily use and nobody asks what changed. AI has made that failure more common, because demos are now cheap to build. AI tools can also change after launch, and their failures are hard to see. This paper sets out the evidence the business needs before ordinary users, data, and pressure are allowed to depend on it.
