entries.title: Confident and wrong
entries.summary: A fluent AI answer can pass a quick read while carrying a mistake nobody checks, and "have a human review it" does not say who looks, at what, or with the power to say no. What does review need to catch it?
entries.metaDescription: A fluent AI answer can pass a quick read while wrong. A five-part challenge protocol: name the decision, break the answer, check outside it, name a reviewer, learn.
entries.operatingMove: Before AI output feeds a decision that matters, run five checks. Name the decision it could change. Try to break the answer. Check its claims outside the answer. Name a reviewer who can say no, with a route past them. Learn from the errors caught.
entries.preview: A fluent AI answer can look finished while carrying a mistake nobody checks. This field note states the paper's working claim, that an answer matching what the reader expected gets less scrutiny, and what that claim rests on. It sets out the five-part challenge protocol and which parts depend on each other, what the studies of fluent AI errors showed and where they stop, four objections, and the one number to watch and when to doubt it.
inside: The five-part challenge protocol, from naming the decision to learning from the errors caught
What the studies of fluent AI errors showed, and where they stop
Four objections, including that nothing yet proves the protocol works
sourcesHtml: Raymond S. Nickerson, "Confirmation Bias: A Ubiquitous Phenomenon in Many Guises," Review of General Psychology 2, no. 2 (1998): 175-220 — A review of research on confirmation bias, the tendency to seek or read evidence in ways that favor beliefs a person already holds. It does not study AI answers.

Mrinank Sharma, Meg Tong, Tomasz Korbak, David Duvenaud, Amanda Askell, Samuel R. Bowman, et al., "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models," arXiv:2310.13548, published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024 — Anthropic researchers found that human preference data favored responses matching a user's views, and that non-expert raters without fact-checking tools sometimes preferred a convincing agreeable answer over a correct one. It does not measure how closely people check AI answers.
OpenAI, "Sycophancy in GPT-4o: What Happened and What We’re Doing About It," April 2025 — OpenAI's account of one April 2025 GPT-4o update that it rolled back as overly flattering or agreeable.

Ziwei Ji, Nayeon Lee, Rita Frieske, et al., "Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation," ACM Computing Surveys, 2023 — A survey of hallucination in language-generation research: output that is fluent and coherent but unfaithful or nonsensical.

Matthew Dahl, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun, and Daniel E. Ho, "Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models," Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1), 2024, 64–93; open version arXiv:2401.01301 — Four 2023 models answered questions about random federal court cases. ChatGPT 4 was inconsistent with legal fact on 58 percent of the questions and Llama 2 on 88 percent. One field, and the models have since been replaced.

Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey, "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration," Human Factors 52, no. 3 (2010): 381–410 — A review of research on automation complacency and automation bias, which appear in experts as well as novices; training or instructions do not prevent automation bias.

Manshu Khanna, Ziyi Wang, Lijia Wei, and Lian Xue, "When Medical AI Explanations Help and When They Harm," arXiv:2512.08424, 2025 — An unreviewed preprint with 257 medical students at one hospital. AI explanations raised accuracy by 6.3 percentage points when the AI was right and lowered it by 4.9 when it was wrong.

Blake Bullwinkel et al., "Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products," Microsoft Research, January 2025 — Lessons from Microsoft's red teaming of more than 100 generative AI products, including that finding failures takes people with expertise and judgment.
entries.bodyHtml:
Fluent AI output can enter work that matters carrying more confidence than evidence, and "have a human review it" often does not catch the problem. This paper takes a position: output that could change a decision or an action that matters should pass a five-part challenge protocol before anyone depends on it.

I have reviewed generated analysis that looked excellent: clean structure, plausible figures, and cited sources. One number felt slightly convenient, so I opened the cited report. The report existed. The number did not. The model had blended two adjacent statistics into one that said what the narrative needed, and nothing in the document gave that away. The only signal was that it agreed with us a little too well.

The hardest AI error to catch is not nonsense; nonsense filters itself. It is the answer that is coherent, specific, and shaped to what the reader expected, and wrong in a way that survives a quick read. The paper's working claim is that an answer that confirms what someone already thinks gets less scrutiny than one that argues back. That claim is an inference. It builds on the long-studied tendency called confirmation bias and on Anthropic research in which people's preference ratings favored answers that matched a user's views. No study cited here measures how closely people check an AI answer at work.

The failure itself is documented. A 2024 study asked four models from 2023 about random federal court cases. ChatGPT 4 gave answers inconsistent with legal fact on 58 percent of the questions and Llama 2 on 88 percent. Those models have been replaced, so the study shows the rate can be high where the stakes are real, not what it is today. In an unreviewed experiment with 257 medical students, AI explanations raised accuracy by 6.3 percentage points when the AI was right (73 percent of cases) and lowered it by 4.9 when it was wrong (27 percent). They helped overall and hurt exactly when the AI erred.

The parts mostly depend on each other in order. The first decides whether the rest apply and how hard. The second feeds the third, because what the attempt to break the answer turns up is the first list of claims to check. The fifth learns from what the others recorded, so it comes last. The one exception is the reviewer for high-stakes output, who is named right after the first part because that person runs the second and third.

Name the decision it could change

A one-minute use declaration before review, which is a planning estimate: which decision, affecting whom, how reversible, at what cost if it is wrong, what the requester expected the answer to say, and for what use, whether brainstorming, drafting, a recommendation, or the basis for an action. Low-stakes uses stop here. Scrutiny concentrates where the stakes do.

Try to break the answer

Before strengthening the answer, try to break it. What would make it false? What other explanation fits the same facts? Who would dispute it, and why? Break hardest where the answer matches what the requester expected. A conclusion that has only survived attempts to improve it has earned nothing yet.

Check the claims outside the answer

Follow the claims the decision rests on to ground outside the answer. Open the cited report. Re-run the calculation. Read the clause itself. Asking the model whether it is sure only consults the same witness again; everything inside the answer is testimony from that one witness.

Name a reviewer, and a route past them

Review works when a named person owns what happens to the output, with relevant expertise, protected time, and the standing to stop the work, and has a defined route for what exceeds them. Volume caps come before generation growth. A reviewer clearing dozens of items a day signs without checking.

Learn from the errors you catch

Every catch is operating evidence. Keep a light failure log, review repeated failures monthly, and give someone authority to change prompts, data, permissions, or review tiers. Otherwise the organization keeps paying for the same lesson in near misses.

Put the five questions in the interface or the work record where people actually depend on the output. Start with one workflow where the stakes are real. The early weeks may turn up catches nobody expected; that is the baseline being found. Then watch one number: how often an outside check changes a claim. It is the share of checked claims that turned out wrong or unsupported, not the workflow's overall error rate, and no source here says how large it should be. If it stays near zero in a tier, test the checkers first with planted known-bad items or a sampled re-check; loosen only if they catch them.

The protocol is the paper's own design, and no study tests it. The white paper answers four objections (distrust, better models, speed, and proof), develops each part with how it typically fails and what counters that, covers the ways a review gets faked (forms filled in by rote, checking the answer against itself, approval in name only), and gives a starter failure log.

entries.title: A portfolio needs scenarios, not a single annual plan
entries.summary: An annual plan cannot say what to do when one of its own assumptions breaks. Keep two alternative versions of the portfolio beside it, each with a signal someone can watch and first moves agreed in advance, so leaders choose from prepared alternatives.
entries.metaDescription: Keep two workable alternatives beside the annual plan. Give each a trigger someone can watch, one owner, and a first move you can undo.
entries.operatingMove: Pick one portfolio where people and dependencies are scarce. Compose two alternatives you could run beside the plan, name one owner and one visible trigger for each, and agree a first move you can reverse.
entries.preview: A hiring freeze arrives after the plan is approved, and the plan has no answer for it. This paper keeps the annual plan as the version everyone commits to and adds a small set of scenarios beside it. Each scenario is an alternative portfolio tested against scarce people and dependencies, with a trigger someone can watch, an owner, and a first move that can be reversed. It adapts established scenario planning to the portfolio, says what no source shows, and answers the objections and the costs.
inside: Why a plan alone has no answer when an assumption breaks, and what the sources do and do not show
Six parts: uncertainties, alternatives, what each protects, triggers, agreed moves, and a short review
Objections and costs, and the first step to take beside the annual plan
sourcesHtml: Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, Portfolio Management: Fundamental for New Product Success, Stage-Gate International — Cooper and Edgett describe portfolio management for new products as a dynamic decision process in which the list of active projects is constantly updated and revised; it is a practitioner account.

Paul J. H. Schoemaker, Scenario Planning: A Tool for Strategic Thinking, Sloan Management Review 36(2), Winter 1995, 25-40 — Schoemaker's 1995 article describes scenario planning as a disciplined method for imagining possible futures, says it compensates for underprediction and overprediction of change, recommends early indicators for each scenario, and asks that scenarios describe generically different futures; it is written for strategic planning.

Hugh Courtney, Jane Kirkland, and Patrick Viguerie, Strategy Under Uncertainty, McKinsey Quarterly (adapted from Harvard Business Review, November-December 1997) — Courtney, Kirkland, and Viguerie of McKinsey set out how to act at different levels of uncertainty, including a limited set of scenarios, the trigger events that show a market moving toward one, and options and no-regrets moves; it is about business strategy.

Stephen Hall, Dan Lovallo, and Reinier Musters, How to Put Your Money Where Your Strategy Is, McKinsey & Company, March 1, 2012 — McKinsey's study of 1,616 US-listed companies measures capital received by business units: year-to-year correlation of 0.92, higher returns for top reallocators as an association, and lower returns for heavy reallocators over periods under three years. It does not test initiatives.

Robert S. Pindyck, Irreversibility, Uncertainty, and Investment, Journal of Economic Literature 29(3), 1991, 1110-1148; NBER Working Paper 3307, 1990 — Pindyck's analysis of investment under uncertainty says an irreversible commitment gives up the chance to wait for new information, and that the lost chance is part of the cost; it is theory, not a study of portfolios.
entries.bodyHtml:
A hiring freeze lands after the plan is approved. The plan assumed the people it needs, and it says nothing about what to do without them. Leaders call a meeting to reorder the portfolio's priorities, run in a hurry by whoever can attend, while each sponsor defends an initiative. I have supported portfolios that went through this. It is an observation from practice, not a measured finding.

This paper argues that a portfolio needs more than its plan: a small set of scenarios kept beside it. A scenario here is an alternative version of the portfolio, tested in advance so leaders know they could run it. Each one comes with a trigger, a signal someone can observe that tells leaders it is time to choose, and with the first moves leaders agree to make if it fires. The plan stays as the version everyone commits to, so "not a single plan" means not a plan alone. No source reviewed here compares portfolios that prepared alternatives with portfolios that re-planned after the surprise. The claim rests on reasoning and on existing methods, not on a measured result.

A re-forecast tells you what changed, not what to do by Friday. Only an alternative composed beforehand does. Scenario planning is an established method for preparing such answers. Paul Schoemaker describes it as a way to imagine possible futures that compensates for under- and overprediction of change. Hugh Courtney and his McKinsey coauthors pair a limited set of scenarios with trigger events to watch. Both write about strategy. This paper adapts the idea to the portfolio: alternatives composed against scarce people and dependencies, a named owner for each trigger, and first moves agreed in advance. That adaptation is untested as a whole.

Most parts hang on the alternatives. Start with two or three uncertainties that would change a choice, found by asking each initiative lead which assumption, if it broke, would change their plan. Build two alternatives you could actually run, which means real subtraction: a downside case that keeps every initiative is the same plan with a worse forecast. Give each alternative one page showing what it protects and what it gives up.

Then set triggers someone can see, each with one owner and a threshold chosen by lead time. "Market deterioration" is a mood. "Two straight quarters of pipeline below the planning level" is a fact. Agree the moves in advance, starting with a step you can reverse and the money that pays for it. Review the assumptions briefly, and retire scenarios whose uncertainty has resolved.

A good re-plan may do as well where surprises are slow and the portfolio has slack. The cycle earns its place where people are scarce, dependencies are shared, and decisions are slow. It costs the time to compose the alternatives, a regular check by each trigger owner, a short review, and money held back. The surprise that arrives may not be one you prepared, though composing the alternatives still shows which initiatives carry weight in every future. Sponsors may also bargain over a hypothetical cut, so the agreement is reopened only when a trigger fires or an assumption expires, and the one person with authority to move money and people decides.

Start with one portfolio where people and dependencies are scarce. Compose two honest alternatives first, because the triggers follow from them. Count the emergency reprioritizations, the hurried meetings that reorder priorities after a shock, for a year before you start. Then ask the first time a trigger fires: did leaders start from the prepared alternatives, or did the old emergency meeting come back? If no trigger fires, run the test on paper using the last real surprise.

The white paper covers what one plan costs when it breaks, the test that separates a scenario from a slide, trigger and move design, a vendor-risk illustration run from start to finish, and the objections and costs in full.

entries.title: Decision friction is a portfolio risk
entries.summary: Consider an invented late program. Its post-mortem lists estimation, complexity, and the vendor. Then someone walks the calendar and finds five weeks spent waiting on a policy question, a tradeoff, or an owner who was never named.
entries.metaDescription: Delay can trace to decisions nobody owns. A decision inventory records the choice, its owner, the evidence needed, and the last useful date.
entries.operatingMove: Keep a list of the choices the work is waiting on. For each one, record what has to be decided, who decides it, what evidence could change the decision, the last useful date, what stops if it slips, and what was finally decided.
entries.preview: Portfolios track work, dates, spend, and risk, but the decisions that hold up that work often stay scattered across meetings, inboxes, and personal notes. When nobody can see the queue, nobody manages it. This paper makes it visible: the choice, its owner, the evidence still needed, the last useful date, the work waiting on it, and what was finally decided. It helps leaders tell a real delivery problem from a question that was simply allowed to drift.
inside: Why the weeks lost waiting on a decision can be blamed on estimation or the vendor
How to record the choice, its owner, the evidence needed, and the last useful date
What a visible queue reveals about bottlenecks and unclear authority
sourcesHtml: Project Management Institute
Mary K. Pratt
De Smet
Blenko
Blenko
entries.bodyHtml:
Portfolios track work, dates, spend, and risk. The decisions that control the work often remain scattered across meetings, inboxes, and personal notes. When no one sees the queue, no one manages it.

Consider an invented late program, offered as an illustration and not as a reported case. Its post-mortem starts with estimation, complexity, or vendor performance. Then someone walks through the calendar and finds five weeks spent waiting for a policy decision, a funding answer, or an owner who was never named. The question was raised early. It moved through several forums, gathered opinions, and produced no decision.

Decision friction is the time and effort required to turn a recognized question into an answer the work can use. It becomes a portfolio risk when teams wait, restate the question, or build against assumptions while the answer is pending. The research cited is general, and the link to portfolio risk is this paper's reading.

Use one visible inventory for decisions that matter. Each entry should state the choice, name the person who can make it, identify the evidence that could change it, set a latest useful date, show the work at risk, and record the outcome.

Write down one answerable choice. "Architecture concerns" is a theme. "Extend the billing platform or adopt the vendor module for the mid-market by March" gives a forum something it can decide.

Assign the decision to the person with authority over the area in dispute. A committee may advise; it is the owner only when its charter gives it authority to decide. A distribution list is a notification channel, never an owner.

Before commissioning more analysis, ask whether a plausible result could change the choice. If it cannot, the analysis only extends the queue. When uncertainty is real, record it and make the tradeoff between more information and more waiting explicit.

Work backward from the first commitment that depends on the answer. The latest useful date is the last point at which the decision can still change the work. "This choice loses its cheapest option on April 12" gives the forum a concrete consequence of delay.

Show the investments, constrained roles, and dependencies waiting on the answer. The same policy question blocking three programs is not three separate project issues. It is one portfolio bottleneck.

Record the answer, the reasoning, the caveats, and the evidence that would justify reopening it. Then confirm that affected owners have updated their plans. A decision is complete when the work changes, not when the meeting ends.

The inventory turns a vague delay into a specific management problem. An aging queue can reveal that a particular forum is too slow, a decision right is unclear, or a recurring question should become standing policy. It also protects teams from the opposite mistake: treating every request for speed as a reason to skip needed evidence or review.

Ask each program lead for the three questions holding up work today. Start with the ones that cross team lines, tie up constrained capacity, set precedent, or are hard to reverse. Review aging decisions and approaching dates inside the existing portfolio forum. A separate decision board often creates another queue.

The inventory cannot make leaders choose between competing priorities. It can make the cost of waiting visible: this decision, this owner, this date, and this work held up. That is enough to make an avoidable delay governable.

entries.title: A PMO dashboard should show investment health
entries.summary: A CFO asks the simplest question about the biggest investment on the page: if we stopped this today, what would we lose? The deck knows the burn rate, the milestone variance, and the issue count. It cannot answer.
entries.metaDescription: A status deck cannot say what you would lose by stopping. A PMO dashboard should show outcome, confidence, capacity, adoption, dependency, and open decisions.
entries.operatingMove: Put six questions on one page per investment. What is the money buying (outcome)? Are the assumptions holding (confidence)? Do the people exist (capacity)? Can the receiving team use it (adoption)? Will outside commitments hold (dependency)? Which decision is due (decision readiness)? Retire any field that has not changed a decision in two review cycles.
entries.preview: A PMO dashboard built from project-tool exports can describe delivery activity well and say little about how the investment is doing. A deck can be accurate in every cell and still leave the one question that matters without a page. This paper defines a page for deciding. It has six lenses, which are six questions asked of every investment: outcome, confidence, capacity, adoption, dependency, and decision readiness. Each lens stays only if its answer changes a decision. The set is a checklist and the paper's own design, with no blended score. The aim is to change the portfolio while there is still time, not to explain the outcome afterward.
inside: Why an accurate status deck cannot answer what you would lose by stopping
Six lenses for each investment: outcome, confidence, capacity, adoption, dependency, and decision readiness
Where the model stops, how to convert the deck you already have, and how to tell the page is working
sourcesHtml: Project Management Institute, "Pulse of the Profession® 2026: Driving Success in Complex Projects," May 2026 — PMI's 2026 survey reports that 61 percent of project professionals experienced some form of value loss on complex projects. The figure is self-reported and concerns complexity, not dashboards.

Michael Bloch, Sven Blumberg, and Jürgen Laartz, "Delivering large-scale IT projects on time, on budget, and on value," McKinsey & Company, October 1, 2012 — McKinsey and Oxford compared predicted and actual budgets, schedules, and benefits for more than 5,400 IT projects. For large ones the averages were 45 percent over budget, 7 percent over time, and 56 percent less value than predicted. The three figures are not ranked, and the study does not say whether projects on budget delivered the value.

U.S. Government Accountability Office, "IT Dashboard: Agencies Are Managing Investment Risk, but Related Ratings Need to Be More Accurate and Available," GAO-14-64, December 12, 2013 — GAO checked 80 federal IT investments on the IT Dashboard against their supporting documents: 53 risk ratings were consistent, 20 partly, and 7 not. Late updates and differing ways of tracking performance were among the causes.

Occupational Safety and Health Administration, "Using Leading Indicators to Improve Safety and Health Outcomes," U.S. Department of Labor — OSHA defines leading indicators as proactive, preventive measures and lagging indicators as measures of events that already happened. The setting is workplace safety, and the paper borrows the terms for investments.

Bent Flyvbjerg, "Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View," 2013 — Flyvbjerg reports that front-end estimates of costs and benefits typically differ significantly from actual results, so they predict value and viability poorly. His evidence comes mostly from large public projects.
entries.bodyHtml:
Here is a scene I have watched play out in a portfolio review. The deck is long and accurate in every cell. Near the end, a CFO asks a simple question about the largest investment on the page: if we stopped this today, what would we actually lose?

Nobody can answer from the deck. It knows the burn rate, the milestone variance, and the issue count. It does not know what the money is still expected to buy, how confident anyone is, or what decision would change the outcome.

A deck built from whatever the project tools can export can look like that one. It describes delivery activity honestly and supports investment decisions poorly.

Status asks: is the work proceeding as planned? Health asks: is this still a good use of money, people, and attention? A project can be green on plan and dead on value. It can be red on plan and still the best available path to an outcome that matters. A McKinsey and Oxford study of large IT projects measured the shortfall in value separately from the cost and schedule overruns. A page that tracks only cost and schedule has no place to show it.

One page per investment, built from six lenses. A lens is a question asked of every investment, kept only because its answer changes a decision a leader can still make. The six are a checklist by design, and they are this paper's own design. The paper does not claim they are the only set.

Outcome health

What operating result is the money buying, and is that path still believable? Delivery progress is not value progress. A build can be eighty percent complete while the need has changed. The decision is continue, reshape, or stop, judged on what remains to gain against what remains to spend, never on money already spent.

Confidence health

Are the case's premises rising, stable, falling, or untested as evidence lands? A forecast quoted to the same decimal for six review cycles has not been tested again. The decision is sizing: expand the commitment where confidence has been earned, and bound the next round of funding where it has not.

Capacity health

Do the people this investment assumes actually exist for it? An investment that depends on unavailable scarce people is unhealthy even when its schedule still looks recoverable. The decision is a portfolio one: sequence the work, narrow it, or release capacity on purpose.

Adoption and operating health

Is the receiving operation becoming able to use and sustain the change? Prefer what it did to what it said: procedures changed, pilot users returning unprompted, a support rota staffed by its own people. The decision is how to roll out: slow it, stage it, or reinforce the receiving side.

Dependency and risk health

Every material dependency with an owner, what must be in place, a latest useful date (the last point at which the commitment can still change the work), and a consequence if it fails. One case this lens targets is the dependency that slips again and again while the forecast never changes. The decision is timing: invoke a fallback while the alternative still exists.

Decision readiness

What choice does this investment need, from whom, by when, and what does waiting cost? Each open decision is an entry from a decision inventory, covered in the paper on decision friction. The paper expects that a forum that opens with the queue spends its time deciding, and one that opens with status spends it being briefed.

Convert the deck you already have by pruning first. Retire any field that has not changed a decision in two review cycles. Then put the six lenses on one page per investment, starting with the largest, and let the page replace that investment's status slides. No composite score: the disagreements between lenses are the information.

The white paper works through each lens, reads an invented investment through the view, sets out where the model stops, gives the conversion steps, and lists the signals that show whether the page is steering.

entries.title: The EPMO's job is capacity, not calendars
entries.summary: Every project has a date and every plan looks solid on its own. Even so, the same few people, systems, and approval forums turn up in all of them. Each plan is fine. The sum is fiction.
entries.metaDescription: Every plan looks sound alone while the same scarce people appear in all of them. Govern EPMO demand against real capacity, not against the calendar.
entries.operatingMove: Govern real demand against the people and systems you actually have, by role, skill, and dependency. The calendar shows what everyone intends to do. The decision is which work gets the scarce capacity and which work waits.
entries.preview: A portfolio calendar shows when activity is planned. It does not show whether the organization has the scarce roles, skills, attention, and dependency capacity to deliver it. This paper puts the EPMO's attention on active demand and the capacity that constrains it, and gives leaders a way to expose overload, compare tradeoffs, and decide which commitments move, change scope, or wait.
inside: Why every plan can be sound on its own and the sum still impossible
How to model the roles, skills, and approval forums that actually constrain delivery
How to present choices about what waits, instead of one plan that cannot hold

Stephen Hall et al.

entries.title: Give stage gates teeth by shrinking what they decide
entries.summary: A gate has teeth only over a choice that is still open: the next hard-to-reverse commitment of money, people, or contracts.
entries.metaDescription: A gate that cannot stop anything is a status meeting. Stage gates govern only when they carry real authority to redirect, pause, or kill a project.
entries.operatingMove: Test one mid-sized gate. List the project's commitments, review the next costly one on its own, and confirm that money and people move with the decision.
entries.preview: A board that votes yes on the whole project has little left to decide once contracts are signed and other programs plan around the result. This paper shows how to find the next commitment, what the board needs to decide it, and how to let an approval run out.
inside: Why a yes to the whole project is hard to take back
How to find the next commitment and review it on its own
How to test one gate before changing the whole process
sourcesHtml: Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, Stage-Gate and the Critical Success Factors for New Product Development, BPTrends — Cooper and Edgett, who founded Stage-Gate Inc., describe incremental commitment, with gates deciding the next stage and its resources, and observe that a project that has begun has very little chance of being killed; this is a practitioner's observation, not a measured rate.

Robert S. Pindyck, “Irreversibility, Uncertainty, and Investment,” Journal of Economic Literature 29(3), 1991, 1110–1148; NBER Working Paper 3307, 1990 — Pindyck's investment theory explains that an irreversible choice gives up the option to wait for more information; it is not a study of project reviews.

Dustin J. Sleesman, Donald E. Conlon, Gerry McNamara, and Jonathan E. Miles, "Cleaning Up the Big Muddy: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Determinants of Escalation of Commitment," Academy of Management Journal 55(3), 2012, 541–562 — This meta-analysis links personal responsibility with escalation of commitment and finds a positive average sunk-cost effect that varies widely; it mostly studies individual decisions, not boards.

Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, "Portfolio Management: Fundamental for New Product Success," Stage-Gate International — Cooper and Edgett describe portfolio management as a dynamic process in which projects can be sped up, killed, or lowered in priority and resources are allocated and re-allocated.

Bent Flyvbjerg, "Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management," 2013 — Flyvbjerg proposes testing a forecast against the actual results of similar projects, because front-end estimates often diverge from what happens.
entries.bodyHtml:
Ask a portfolio board when its last review changed how much money, how many people, or how much scope a project received. If no one can name a case, the review may be tracking progress rather than governing the investment. A board with well-chosen projects may rarely stop anything, so the test is not a count of stops. It is whether the review could have changed what the project received, and whether it ever did. A gate has teeth when it can change what a project receives: its money, its people, or its scope.

Reviews tend to fail in one of two ways. Some lack the authority to act: leaders ask for another slide, and the project keeps its funding, staff, and scope. Others vote yes or no on the whole project, once. A yes given early is hard to take back, because contracts are signed, people are hired, and other programs plan around the result. Research on escalation of commitment, the tendency to keep backing a failing course, also links personal responsibility with greater escalation, although the average effect of money already spent varied widely across studies.

A gate has teeth only over a choice that is still open, so the fix starts with where the gate sits. A stage drawn around a phase of work, such as design or build, can end after the point where reversing a step has become expensive. A gate should sit before the first step that is hard to reverse and decide that step: the next commitment, meaning a step that is hard to reverse because it spends a sum the board would not want to lose, pulls scarce people from other work, signs a contract, or lets other programs plan around the result.

Decide the next commitment, then give the board what it needs

To find the next commitment, list the steps the project will take, in order, and mark each as cheap or costly to reverse. A short test with no contract is cheap. A multi-year contract or a shared platform is costly. Approve the cheap work up to the next costly step, and review that step on its own with stronger evidence in front of it.

Three controls make the decision real. The board has written authority to continue, redirect, narrow, pause, or stop, with the effect of each outcome defined before the meeting. The evidence fits the size of the commitment and sits on a one-page evidence map. Someone other than the sponsor owns the key facts that could change the decision. Each approval then carries an end date, the three or four facts it rests on, and a trigger that sends the decision back to the board.

Test one gate before changing the whole process

Choose one mid-sized decision with real stakes. Write the next commitment in one sentence, and list what each of the five outcomes would do to money, people, scope, and dependencies. Record the decision, the assumptions, the triggers, the end date, and any dissent in the meeting, then check that money and people moved as directed.

After two or three reviews, compare what the board committed at each step with what was requested. If nothing ever changes and the board could not have changed it, fix the authority and the size of the commitment before adding templates. A gate earns its place when evidence can change the next commitment while the organization still has options.

entries.title: A project is not ready because a plan exists
entries.summary: A complete plan can still lack four promises from people outside the delivery team. Before kickoff, check who can decide, what result will count, which people will take part, and whether named staff have time.
entries.metaDescription: A finished plan is not readiness. Confirm four things first: who decides, what the outcome is, who takes part, and who is free to do the work.
entries.operatingMove: Before setting a start date, list the first hard decisions and who can make them. Agree on one result and its limits, confirm the people and dates, then check each person's other work.
entries.preview: A sound schedule and signed charter can hide a sponsor who cannot decide or an expert promised to several projects; four short questions help leaders find those gaps before a team starts work it cannot support.
inside: How a complete plan can hide missing promises
Four questions to ask before kickoff
What to do when one promise is weak
sourcesHtml: Project Management Institute, "Pulse of the Profession 2026: Driving Success in Complex Projects," May 2026 — PMI's 2026 survey describes how complexity affects projects. It does not test this readiness method.

Bent Flyvbjerg, "Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View," 2013 — Flyvbjerg argues for checking early project estimates against an outside view before a decision.

Michael Bloch, Sven Blumberg, and Jürgen Laartz, "Delivering large-scale IT projects on time, on budget, and on value," McKinsey & Company, 2012 — The McKinsey-Oxford study reports average cost and value gaps in large IT projects. It does not assign those gaps to this paper's four checks.

Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, "Portfolio Management: Fundamental for New Product Success," Stage-Gate International — Cooper and Edgett describe new-product portfolio management as a series of choices to select, rank, speed up, or stop work.

Marcia W. Blenko and Michael C. Mankins, "Measuring Decision Effectiveness," Bain & Company, June 5, 2012 — Bain reports a link between decision effectiveness and financial results; that link does not validate this readiness method.
entries.bodyHtml:
I have watched projects arrive at kickoff with a sound schedule, a signed charter, and supportive leaders in the room, yet still be unready to start.

The missing pieces were promises from people outside the delivery team: who would settle the first hard decision, and which result would guide that choice? Which business experts would join design and testing, and did the named architect have hours left after the meeting ended?

In this paper's reading, a kickoff date creates its own momentum, because once invitations go out, asking whether the project should start can sound like obstruction. Leaders should test readiness before the date goes on the calendar, while the sponsor still has to explain why the project can start.

The sponsor should answer four questions with proof a reviewer can check before leaders grant the project a start date. The questions look past the plan to the people and choices on which that plan depends.

Can the sponsor decide?

The sponsor must be able to settle the choices the project will face, or confirm that another leader will take the question. Before kickoff, list the first three or four hard decisions and write down who can make each one. A sponsor who avoids naming those choices may lack the authority the project needs.

What result will count?

Name one result the business can test and state what this stage of work leaves out. "Implement the platform" names a product, but it does not say what should improve after people use it. The person who will live with the result should agree to the result and its limits in writing.

Will the right people take part?

Support in a meeting does not reserve anyone's time, so name the experts needed for workshops, tests, data checks, and the handover. Set dates their managers can confirm. Forty names on a list may be useful for communication; six people with confirmed hours tell leaders whether the work can start.

Do named staff have time?

Check the architect, product owner, data expert, and other scarce roles against work already under way. Consider a test lead named in several approved plans that each look sound alone. Together, the plans may ask for more hours than one person has, and no one has added the assignments across projects.

Three firm promises cannot make up for one hopeful answer, because a sponsor with authority but no clear result may make a fast choice about the wrong thing. A clear result will not help if business experts never join the work, so reviewers should press hardest on the weakest answer.

Run the review before kickoff with the sponsor, the person who owns the result, and the person who can settle staff conflicts. Leaders can start, reduce the work, fund a short discovery stage, or wait, but they should record why they chose that path. Review the four promises again if a key person, result, or promised date changes.

A readiness review may take time, but an unsupported start may create more delay. Measure speed from approval to the first useful result, and track which missing promises caused projects to need a new start. Those records tell leaders whether the review saved time and which question needs to change.

entries.title: Build one evidence record for the AI decision and your part in it
entries.summary: A sponsor deciding on an AI program asks what can be inspected. A later employer or promotion panel asks what you personally did. Program documents describe the service, not your choices, and memory favors the person remembering. The paper recommends one record, written while the program runs and checked by others.
entries.metaDescription: A sponsor asks what can be inspected, and a later employer asks what you did. One evidence record, written while an AI program runs, can answer both.
entries.operatingMove: Before the next decision that matters, pick one claim and fill in six fields: the claim, the context and work, the evidence, the result or learning, the limits, and the owner and next decision. Give the sponsor the record before the meeting, have someone outside the program check it, and narrow or hold any claim the evidence cannot support.
entries.preview: The sponsor's question comes first: what can we inspect that shows this works outside the demonstration? A later reader asks something different, namely what you did. This field note describes one record that serves both, why program documents and memory fall short for the second, and what the record costs. It states the objections, including confidentiality, and what no source tests.
entries.bodyHtml:
Suppose you lead an AI program and your next funding decision is close. The demonstration works. The sponsor, the executive who approves the money, asks: What can we inspect that shows this works outside the demonstration, for which uses, and who answers for it? Later, another employer, a promotion panel, or a client will ask what you personally did and what came of it.

This paper expects that two beliefs carry a leader through both questions. One is that the program's own documents will answer them. The other is that you will remember what you did. Neither holds up well. The usual documents describe the AI service and how it is managed, not who made each decision, and memory favors the person remembering.

This paper recommends one record, written while the program runs and built around a single claim the decision depends on. The sponsor reads it to decide about the program. Later, you draw a short statement of your own part from it. A personal file of achievements may not be checked by anyone. This record is read and tested by other people while the work is fresh. No study tests whether such a record changes a funding decision or a hiring outcome, so it is this paper's design, not a proven method.

The program's documents describe the service, not your choices

"The Demo-to-Production Gap" covers the written approval for the AI tool itself. The record here is the working file that supplies the evidence behind such an approval, and it adds a trail of who made which choice. Published guidance offers categories for a record about an AI service: purpose, performance, monitoring, incident response, and documented responsibility. Examples are FactSheets, NIST's Generative AI Profile and AI Risk Management Framework, and the GAO's accountability framework. None of it shows that buyers or boards use those categories, and none records which person made which choice.

Memory favors the person remembering

Ross and Sicoly ran five experiments with married couples, students, and basketball players. People recalled more of their own contributions to joint work than of the others', and they claimed more responsibility than the others credited to them. The studies did not cover workplaces or leaders, so the result is a warning, not a measurement. In one experiment, notes did not clearly change who people credited, and the authors suspected the notes were too brief. This paper infers that the record should tie each choice to the decision it shaped and name the other contributors.

What the later reader looks for is only partly known. In LinkedIn's own survey of 1,271 recruiting professionals, 93 percent said that accurately assessing a candidate's skills is crucial for improving the quality of a hire. That shows only that recruiters rate skills assessment as important.

One claim, six fields

You write the record, the sponsor reads it, and you update it at each decision. Pick the claim by asking whether the sponsor would decide differently if it were false. Then fill in six fields. They are the claim, which is about the program; the context and work, including who made each choice and who else contributed; the evidence itself; the result or learning; the limits; and the owner and next decision.

A weak field means evidence exists but covers little, so the claim is narrowed to what the evidence covers. A missing field means no evidence exists yet, so the claim stays out of the decision and out of any later account until it does. A limits field left empty counts as missing. Someone outside the program checks the claim against its evidence, and the people named confirm their entries.

What can go wrong

The record shows the sponsor where your evidence stops and what went wrong, and the paper cannot remove that cost. Confidential work stays private, anonymized, or described through a method. The record belongs to the program and the employer, so check the confidentiality terms with a manager or legal contact before keeping a copy or sharing a statement of your part. A record can be gamed or turn into paperwork, so attach the evidence itself and treat an empty limits field as missing. As planning estimates, not measurements, expect about two hours to set up one record and about fifteen minutes to update it, plus short checks by others. Nothing here shows the record works, and credentials, reputation, and trusted relationships continue to matter.

What to do next

Before the next decision that matters, pick one claim and fill in the six fields. Give the sponsor the record before the meeting. Narrow or hold any claim the evidence cannot support. When you leave the program, write a short statement of your own part from the record while it is still in front of you.
inside: Why program documents and memory both fall short of what a later reader asks
The six fields of the record, who checks it, and what a weak or a missing field means
The objections: exposure, confidentiality, paperwork, cost, and what no source shows
sourcesHtml: Matthew Arnold, Rachel K. E. Bellamy, Michael Hind, Stephanie Houde, Sameep Mehta, Aleksandra Mojsilović, Ravi Nair, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Darrell Reimer, Alexandra Olteanu, David Piorkowski, Jason Tsay, and Kush R. Varshney, "FactSheets: Increasing Trust in AI Services through Supplier's Declarations of Conformity," arXiv:1808.07261, submitted August 22, 2018, revised February 7, 2019 — a research team proposed FactSheets, a document the supplier fills in to describe an AI service's purpose, performance, safety, security, and provenance. It is a proposal, not a study of adoption.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 2024 — NIST's Generative AI Profile suggests voluntary actions for monitoring, evaluation, and incident response across an AI system's life. It does not prescribe a record.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — NIST's AI Risk Management Framework Core asks organizations to document roles and responsibilities for managing AI risk and to plan periodic review. It is voluntary and does not cover one person's account of their part.

U.S. Government Accountability Office, "Artificial Intelligence: An Accountability Framework for Federal Agencies and Other Entities," GAO-21-519SP, June 30, 2021 — the U.S. Government Accountability Office lists governance, data, performance, and monitoring practices for managers, auditors, and third-party assessors of AI systems. It offers categories, not evidence that organizations use them.

Michael Ross and Fiore Sicoly, "Egocentric Biases in Availability and Attribution," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 37(3), 322-336, 1979 — five experiments with married couples, student groups, basketball players, and graduate students found that people recall more of their own contributions to joint work and claim more responsibility than others credit them. In one experiment, notes did not clearly change who people credited, and asking students about their supervisors first shifted credit toward the supervisors. The studies did not cover workplaces or leaders.

Greg Lewis, "LinkedIn Report: How AI Will Redefine Recruiting in 2025," LinkedIn Talent Blog, February 13, 2025 — LinkedIn's research team surveyed 1,271 recruiting professionals, and 93 percent said accurately assessing a candidate's skills is crucial for improving quality of hire. This is LinkedIn's own research on its members. It records a belief, not that a record changes a hiring decision.

entries.title: Portfolio governance is a funding-discipline problem, not a reporting problem
entries.summary: A portfolio review can have an accurate dashboard and still be unable to say why one project was funded ahead of another. The fix is funding discipline, not better reporting. Funding discipline is the authority, the evidence, and the willingness to start, continue, redirect, or stop a project.
entries.metaDescription: A review that only reports cannot say why it funded one project over another. Ask whether it could have changed what a project received.
entries.operatingMove: Before the next review, collect one page from each project that asks for money or people. Afterward, ask of each project: could this review have changed what it received, and did it?
entries.preview: A portfolio review can describe every project accurately and still not govern the portfolio. This paper sets out three things a review needs in order to decide, and a question that tests whether yours did. It describes the page every project files, the capacity ledger, and the decision record that a portfolio management office keeps. It also says where the argument is weaker.
inside: The three things a review needs in order to decide: authority, evidence, and willingness
A question that tests a review without counting stops
The page every project files, the capacity ledger, and the decision record the PMO keeps
sourcesHtml: Project Management Institute, The Standard for Portfolio Management, Third Edition, 2013 — PMI's standard defines portfolio governance as a governing body making investment and priority decisions, describes the review meeting as the place to decide, and lists the roles a PMO may take; it is a professional standard, not a study of outcomes.

Stephen Hall, Dan Lovallo, and Reinier Musters, "How to Put Your Money Where Your Strategy Is," McKinsey & Company, March 1, 2012 — McKinsey's study of 1,616 US-listed companies found the capital each business unit received correlated 0.92, on average, from one year to the next; it measures business-unit capital, not projects. It also found higher shareholder returns for top-third reallocators over 15 years and lower returns for heavy reallocators over spans under three years.

Robert G. Cooper and Scott J. Edgett, "Portfolio Management: Fundamental for New Product Success," Stage-Gate International — Cooper and Edgett define portfolio management as a dynamic decision process and note that projects at different stages must be compared on different amounts of information; it is a practitioner account, not a measured result.

Dustin J. Sleesman, Donald E. Conlon, Gerry McNamara, and Jonathan E. Miles, "Cleaning Up the Big Muddy: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Determinants of Escalation of Commitment," Academy of Management Journal 55(3), 2012, 541–562 — A meta-analysis of 35 years of escalation-of-commitment research links personal responsibility for the original choice to more escalation; most of the studies cover individual decisions, not review groups.

Bent Flyvbjerg, "Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management," 2013 — Flyvbjerg reports that front-end estimates of cost and benefit often differ significantly from actual results, drawing mostly on large transportation projects, and proposes checking a proposal against similar completed projects.

Johannes-Tobias Lorenz, Joshan Cherian Abraham, Robert Levin, and Douglas Ziman, "From promise to impact: How companies can measure—and realize—the full value of AI," McKinsey & Company, April 24, 2026 — McKinsey's article describes recurring evidence packs and decision gates for AI use cases, with only those that prove value advancing to scale; it is a consulting argument, not a measured result.
entries.bodyHtml:
A portfolio review can have an accurate dashboard and still be unable to say why one project was funded ahead of another. Every project has a status color, a milestone date, and a budget line. The members leave informed, but no one can point to evidence that compared the projects. This paper argues that such a review needs funding discipline, not better reporting. Funding discipline is the authority, the evidence, and the willingness to start, continue, redirect, or stop a project. The claim follows from how the Project Management Institute defines portfolio governance: a group that makes decisions about investments and priorities. Reporting is the first half of that job. A review can finish it and never start the second.

A review needs three things in order to decide. Its members need the authority to move money and people, not only recommend. They need evidence that lets them compare projects, which is hard because projects sit at different stages and compete for the same resources. They also need the willingness to stop a project that is visible, sponsored, and already expensive. Authority and willingness belong to the executives on the review. Evidence is the one a portfolio management office (PMO) can mostly build. A question tests a review: could it have changed what a project received, and did it? If every project deserves what it asked for, a review will change little, so a no is a prompt to find which of the three was missing. The paper does not score a review by its number of stops.

The paper's remedy is one page that every project files each time it asks for money or people. It gives the outcome and the evidence that it is changing, the value expected and shown, the capacity the project holds, the criteria for stopping or redirecting it, and the owner. The PMO keeps that page comparable, keeps a ledger of the scarce people each approved project holds, and keeps a record of what each review decided. The paper also covers where the argument is weaker: a PMO without backing from the member who runs the review, a page that favors what can be measured, and sources that do not show what weak funding discipline costs.

entries.title: The limit on AI agents may be the people who supervise them
entries.summary: Every AI agent adds work that a named person must review, own, and explain. Oversight may be the first limit a company hits, and a plan can easily leave it uncounted.
entries.metaDescription: Oversight may be the first limit on AI agents. Count the review work behind each agent, match review to risk, and keep live AI work within what owners can supervise.
entries.operatingMove: Log one workflow's review hours beside its live volume for four weeks, then widen or narrow the number of live agents before adding another.
entries.preview: AI agents can produce work in seconds, and people need time to check it. Oversight may become the first limit a company hits. This paper shows leaders how to estimate how much AI work one person can supervise (the span of supervision), what to do when no estimate is possible, how to review by risk, and how to fund review time for every AI workflow. It also says where the evidence stops.
inside: How to estimate how much AI work one person can own
How risk-based review and automated controls extend a team
What the evidence supports, and where it stops
sourcesHtml: Alexander Sukharevsky, Alexis Krivkovich, Arne Gast, Arsen Storozhev, Dana Maor, Deepak Mahadevan, Lari Hämäläinen, and Sandra Durth, "The agentic organization: Contours of the next paradigm for the AI era," McKinsey & Company, September 26, 2025 — McKinsey's authors forecast that human oversight will cap how widely companies adopt AI agents, and say that in their experience a team of two to five can supervise 50 to 100 agents. No sample or method is given, so the paper does not treat the figure as a benchmark.

M. L. Cummings and P. J. Mitchell, "Operator Scheduling Strategies in Supervisory Control of Multiple UAVs," Aerospace Science and Technology 11 (2007): 339–348 — Cummings and Mitchell report cognitive saturation and automation bias in a simulation with one operator supervising several semi-autonomous unmanned aircraft; the study did not measure performance as aircraft were added.

M. L. Cummings and Stephanie Guerlain, “Developing Operator Capacity Estimates for Supervisory Control of Autonomous Vehicles,” Human Factors 49, no. 1 (2007): 1–15 — Cummings and Guerlain report lower performance and awareness at 16 missiles, with 8 and 12 also tested, in one simulation with 42 U.S. Navy personnel; the result does not set a business AI limit.

David Mallon, Brad Kreit, and Natasha Buckley, "Rethinking operating models for humans with agents," Deloitte Insights, April 2, 2026 — Deloitte says oversight may include agents guarding other agents that are then guarded by humans.

Chloe Autio, Reva Schwartz, Jesse Dunietz, Shomik Jain, Martin Stanley, Elham Tabassi, Patrick Hall, and Kamie Roberts, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024 — The NIST Generative AI Profile suggests ongoing monitoring, red-team exercises, independent evaluation, incident response, and structured feedback.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — The NIST AI RMF Core organizes AI risk work into govern, map, measure, and manage functions and treats monitoring as ongoing.

Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich H. Manzey, "Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration," Human Factors 52, no. 3 (2010): 381–410 — Parasuraman and Manzey review mostly laboratory evidence that people monitor automation less closely when other tasks compete for attention and the automation is consistently reliable; the studies do not set an enterprise AI staffing ratio.
entries.bodyHtml:
You are told to add more AI agents, find more uses, and get more work done. The plan may count model cost and technical skill. It may not ask a harder question: How many AI decisions can your people still review, explain, and stand behind?

Every agent adds output. It also adds work for people who check important results, handle exceptions, and answer when the AI is wrong. The claim here is narrow: human oversight can become the first limit a company hits as it adds agents, and a plan can easily leave it uncounted. The evidence does not show that it always does, and it gives no number a company can borrow. If the owner's review hours stay well within the time the owner has as agents or cases are added to a workflow, oversight is not the limit for that workflow.

McKinsey's authors expect human oversight to cap how widely companies adopt AI agents. They also say that, in their experience, a team of two to five people can already supervise 50 to 100 specialized agents. That is a forecast and an early observation with no stated method, not a safe benchmark. It still points to the question leaders need to answer: Where is the limit for this team and this work?

Estimate how much one person can supervise

The span of supervision is how much AI work one accountable person can genuinely own, counted in one unit per workflow, such as agents, cases a week, or decisions. The span gets smaller when errors are costly, hard to see, or hard to reverse. It can be larger when errors are easy to spot and fix. If no one can estimate it yet because the workflow is new, start at the narrowest span: one owner, one workflow, a person checking every case or a large sample, and no new agents or cases until the records exist. Widen only after four weeks of records show room.

Use a weekly test. Can the named owner explain what the agent did, what was checked, what failed, and what changed? A no can mean the owner is out of time, or that the records are too thin to answer from. Compare the owner's hours with what the owner expected before narrowing the span. If the hours are fine, fix the records first.

Review by risk

Oversight does not mean reading every output. Low-risk work may need sampling. High-risk work may need a person to approve each case. New or uncertain work may need tighter review until the team knows its typical failures. Write down what is sampled, what always gets checked, what triggers a deeper review, and who can stop the workflow.

Use tools, but keep a human owner

Critic agents, guardrails, monitoring, tests, and incident response can help a small team supervise more work. They can find common errors and send unusual cases to people. They still need their own tests and monitoring. A named person must be able to change or stop them.

Treat review time as shared capacity

Every live AI workflow draws on a shared group of reviewers and experts. Each funding request should name the owner, expected review load, type of review, experts needed for hard cases, and signals that would pause or stop the work. When that pool is full, move attention away from stable, low-risk work before adding more demand.

Start with one workflow

The owner writes a one-page record with the portfolio owner who funds the work. As a planning estimate, not a measured figure, expect a few hours to write it and a few minutes a week to log review time. Each week, log the owner's review and follow-up hours beside the live volume behind them. After four weeks, check whether exceptions reached the right person and whether the owner can explain what changed. If the owner had room, widen the span one step and compare hours before and after. If time ran over, narrow it before another agent goes live.

Better models and automated checks may shrink the review load, and the weekly log will show it if they do. Oversight may not be your limit, but you will not know until you count.

entries.title: Measure AI by the workflow it changes
entries.summary: Usage shows who opened the tool. It does not show whether cycle time, quality, or rework improved.
entries.metaDescription: Measure AI through one recurring workflow: who used it, what result changed, and what evidence shows that AI contributed.
entries.operatingMove: Choose one recurring workflow. Set the baseline, measures, comparison, and four possible decisions before the team sees the result.
entries.preview: AI usage reports show activity, not operating results. This paper links tool use to workflow measures and a practical comparison, then turns the evidence into a choice to continue, hold, change, or stop.

How to set the baseline and evidence rule before the test
How to measure results without watching every employee
