National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), January 2023 — The NIST AI RMF Core calls for analysis, tests, comparison, monitoring, and a record of risks that cannot be measured.

Gartner, "Gartner Survey Finds 45% of Organizations With High AI Maturity Keep AI Projects Operational for at Least Three Years," June 30, 2025 — Gartner reports associations among AI maturity, longer-running projects, business trust, and defined success measures; the survey does not prove causation.
entries.bodyHtml:
Most AI tools can report active users, sessions, and feature use within days. Those numbers answer a useful question: Did people open the tool? They do not answer the question leaders funded the program to solve: Did recurring work get faster, better, or less costly?

In a Gartner survey, 49 percent of respondents named estimating and showing AI value as the main barrier to adoption. A preliminary MIT NANDA study, reported by Fortune, found little or no measurable profit-and-loss effect for most pilots in its dataset. The study was preliminary and the report was secondary, so the figure is a warning, not a universal failure rate.

Measure the workflow in three layers

First, check whether AI reached the people and tasks in the target workflow. Tool-use data shows breadth and concentration. It does not show value by itself.

Second, check whether the workflow result moved. Use records the operation already keeps: cycle time, throughput, errors, rework, escalations, approval time, or another result leaders already care about. Pair speed or volume with quality so a visible gain does not hide later work.

Third, test whether AI is a credible reason for the change. Compare the workflow before and after, compare similar teams, sample quality, or check a manager's account against the records. State what the comparison can and cannot support.

Set the rules before seeing the answer

Name the workflow owner, data owner, and AI program owner. Write the baseline and follow-up periods, the measures, the comparison method, the level of tool use needed for a fair test, and the people who must confirm the result.

End with a choice

Every review should end with one of four choices: continue, hold, change, or stop. Record the choice, owner, reason, next check, and any signal that would reopen it.

Measure without watching every person

Use the least personal data that can answer the workflow question. Avoid keystroke logs, screen recordings, and a record of every prompt. Tell people what is measured, why it matters, who can see it, and which decision it supports.

Start with one recurring workflow

Choose one workflow with enough volume to measure. Ask: Which result changed, by how much, against what baseline, and with what evidence that AI contributed? If the program cannot answer, it may still be a useful experiment. It is not yet proof that the operation improved.

entries.title: Every agent needs a human operating model
entries.summary: A capable AI agent clears its pilot, and the decision to switch it on lands with one leader who will answer for everything it does next. What has to be true before it is allowed to touch real work?
entries.metaDescription: Before an AI agent acts on real work, one named person should answer seven questions about it. A position, with what would show it wrong.
entries.operatingMove: Before funding an agent, have its owner write the Agent Operating-Model Canvas: one answer for each of seven elements, from what the agent may decide to who owns the result. A missing answer holds the funding for real work. Put the owner's time in the budget.
entries.preview: A capable agent clears its pilot and the decision to put it into production lands on one leader. This field note takes a position: before an agent acts on real work, a named person should be able to answer seven questions about it. It says which parts of the list come from Deloitte, what the paper adds (one named owner, a funding gate, a one-page record), how to find the owner and cost the owner's time, and what would show the position wrong.
inside: The Agent Operating-Model Canvas: seven questions a named person answers before an agent acts on real work
How to find the owner and what the owner's time costs
What the evidence does not show, and what would show the position wrong
sourcesHtml: Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, and Michael Chui, with Tara Balakrishnan, "The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation," McKinsey & Company, November 5, 2025 — McKinsey's 2025 survey reports that 88 percent of respondents used AI regularly in at least one business function and 39 percent reported an effect on earnings at the enterprise level.

Gartner, "Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027," press release, June 25, 2025 — Gartner's June 2025 release forecasts that more than 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear value, and weak risk controls. It is a prediction, not a count.

David Mallon, Brad Kreit, and Natasha Buckley, "Rethinking operating models for humans with agents," Deloitte Insights, April 2, 2026 — Deloitte's article names the split of decisions, stop mechanisms, and activity logging, and reports its own survey finding that 84 percent of companies have not redesigned jobs to fit AI. It does not call for one accountable person.

Alexander Sukharevsky, Alexis Krivkovich, Arne Gast, Arsen Storozhev, Dana Maor, Deepak Mahadevan, Lari Hämäläinen, and Sandra Durth, "The agentic organization: Contours of the next paradigm for the AI era," McKinsey & Company, September 26, 2025 — McKinsey's authors describe critic, guardrail, and compliance agents, and people working above the loop, as where agentic organizations are heading, not as current practice.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — The NIST AI RMF Core organizes AI risk work into govern, map, measure, and manage. It is voluntary.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 2024 — The NIST Generative AI Profile suggests monitoring third-party systems in deployment, structured public feedback such as red-teaming, and incident response. It is voluntary.
entries.bodyHtml:
A capable AI agent, software that takes actions on its own, clears its pilot. The decision to put it into production lands on one leader's desk. Approving it means giving the agent a live workflow and letting it act on real customers and real data. At that moment there is no settled answer to a plain question. The agent makes a judgment call, escalates the wrong case, or returns an output that looks finished and is wrong. Who in the organization owns that result?

This paper takes a position: an AI agent should not act on real work until one named person, the owner, can answer seven questions about it. It is a position, not a finding. No source used here compares agents that went live with these answers against agents that went live without them. The position would be wrong for a kind of work if agents with no named owner, no written rules on what they may decide, and no way to halt them made no more costly mistakes than governed ones. This paper expects it to matter least where mistakes are cheap and easy to undo.

Gartner forecasts that more than 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs, unclear business value, or inadequate risk controls. That is a prediction, not a count. Gartner names immature models too, but its other reasons point to how agents are chosen and governed.

The canvas is a one-page sheet with one answer for each of seven elements. Part of it is not new: Deloitte's article already lists three elements, the split of decisions, the stop mechanisms, and the activity logging. This paper adds three things: one named owner who answers for all seven, a funding gate (an agent is not funded for real work until its canvas is complete), and the canvas itself as the written record the gate checks. No source tests whether those additions improve outcomes.

1. Role and scope

What is it for, and where does it stop? Scope creep, where duties widen without a decision, is one way an agent ends up making decisions nobody designed it to make.

2. What it may decide, and what it may not

What may it decide alone, what needs a sign-off, and what must it escalate? If the rule is not written, the agent has the widest authority anyone can read into it.

3. How it escalates and stops

A path for cases it should not handle, and a stop switch that halts it and exists before it is needed. One bad assumption at speed can become many bad outputs.

4. What has to challenge it

Before anyone trusts an output, what checked it, and what did that check catch? Confident wrong answers can be the costly ones.

5. What a good result looks like

Define good before the agent produces anything. Otherwise review collapses into a check for plausibility, which a fluent model can pass without being right.

6. What evidence it leaves

A trail that lets a person work out what the agent did and why. Keeping it is how an organization would turn standards like NIST's into daily practice.

7. Who owns the result

One named person who owns the outcomes. Not a committee. Not the vendor. If no name attaches, the agent should not go live.

The owner is the person who owns the business result of the workflow the agent works in, the one whose target or budget takes the loss when it goes wrong. Test any candidate with four questions. Who takes the loss? Who can change the workflow's rules? Who can stop the agent today without asking anyone? Who has the time? The owner's time is a cost that is easy to leave out of a plan, so it goes in the budget. How many agents one owner can answer for is a separate question, covered in "The Limit on AI Agents May Be the People Who Supervise Them."

Make a completed canvas a requirement for funding real work. The owner writes it, a few sentences per answer, and revises it when the agent's scope, model, or vendor changes. A missing answer holds the funding, and the agent can continue only as a limited test whose output a person checks first. A weak answer narrows what the agent is funded to do.

The white paper works through all seven elements, gives three illustrations, answers the objections, and says what the evidence does not show.

entries.title: Enterprise AI trust is built through operating evidence, not tool novelty
entries.summary: An AI assistant approved for one team's use is not approved for the next team's. The second team can depend on the first team's experience for a use nobody tested, or reopen the whole debate and make every new use as slow as the first. The paper recommends an evidence pack that travels with the system and says what it covers.
entries.metaDescription: An AI tool approved for one use is not approved for the next. Keep an evidence pack that travels with the system and says what it covers.
entries.operatingMove: Pick the system that has one approved use and is likely to get a second. Have its steward assemble the system part of the pack and a register of uses, have the first owner write the use part ending with what it covers, and name a reviewer. When the next team asks, it answers the four questions for its own use.
entries.preview: The first approval answers whether one team may depend on an AI system for one use. The second team's request starts four new questions, and the first team's tests sit in its own files. This field note describes an evidence pack in two parts, one kept for the system and one for each use, with a line on what it does not cover. It names five triggers for testing again, a better model among them. It also gives the objections, the cost as planning estimates, and what no source tests.
entries.bodyHtml:
Consider an AI assistant that drafts summaries of customer contracts for a sales-operations team. A risk reviewer approved that use after the team tested it. Now the procurement team asks to use the same assistant on supplier contracts. The first approval covers customer contracts, and its tests and notes sit in one team's files. The procurement lead can depend on the first team's experience for a use nobody tested, or reopen the whole debate, which makes every new use as slow as the first. This is an illustration, not an account of a real company.

This paper's position is that the proof has to be written so it can travel and be checked again. The record is an evidence pack. In it, the system is the AI assistant or tool itself, and a use is one task for one group of people. The pack says what the system did, on what basis, where it has and has not been tested, and who answers for depending on it, and it is kept current as the system and its uses change. The paper starts after the first approval, which "The Demo-to-Production Gap" covers. In this paper's design, that approval and its tests become the first use's part of the pack, and the second use answers the four questions again plus whichever of that paper's seven production questions, such as ownership or stop authority, the new use changes.

A strong pilot often ends up on low-stakes work at the edge of the business. That is the paper's observation, and no source here counts how often it happens. A tempting response is to ask for a better model. The paper reads the stall differently: the people accountable for important work cannot show that they can depend on the system for that work. A new model is a change like any other, so the tests run on the old one no longer cover it.

This is a reading, not a measured cause. McKinsey's survey found security and risk concerns to be the top barrier to scaling agentic AI, and Deloitte's found that few companies have a mature governance model for autonomous agents. McKinsey asks what holds leaders back and Deloitte asks how mature their governance is. Neither measures why a particular pilot stalled. The reading would be wrong if a pilot with a current pack, a named owner, and tested limits were still kept out of important work, or if a pilot moved into important work on a better model alone, with no new tests.

A use means one task, for one group of people, with one kind of input. For each use, the owner who answers for it has to show four things: what the system did, the basis for its result, where it has and has not been tested, and who answers for depending on it. Because the answers belong to a use, a second use starts with four new questions, and the first team's answers only partly carry over.

The pack has two parts, kept by two people. The system part is true for every use: the version and supplier, what has changed, test results, incident history, and known weak spots. The system steward, the person or team that runs the system for everyone, keeps it and keeps a register of uses. The use part covers one use: the purpose, the cases tested and not tested, how human review works, and the owner. It ends with one line saying what the pack covers and what it does not. A reviewer who did not build the pack reads it against the four questions and tries to find an answer that is missing or untested.

When the second team asks, its owner checks that the system part is current, writes a use part, and tests a sample of its own cases. If all four answers are there, the use goes ahead. If one is missing, the use stays a trial on low-risk work. If one is weak, the use is limited to the cases the tests cover. Nothing here measures how much time the review saves; the paper expects it to look at the differences instead of the whole system.

A pack filed once is a snapshot. The paper sets five triggers for testing again: the system changes, the inputs change, the use widens, something goes wrong, or a fixed interval passes with none of those. A better model is a trigger like the rest. The owner decides what to retest, and the reviewer samples the changes the owner called small. A trigger with no retest behind it counts as a missing answer for whatever it touches. The triggers are the paper's design, drawn on NIST guidance that treats AI risk work as continuous and asks for re-evaluation when a model is adapted to a new domain.

The pack becomes paperwork if no decision ever uses it, so each page must answer one of the four questions. It is not a certification: no single standard governs AI evidence packs, and a complete pack can still sit beside a system used past its tested limits. A small team with one use can write one page and split it when a second use appears. The paper's cost figures are planning estimates, a day or so for the system part and a few days for a use part. No study tests whether packs shorten a second review or reduce incidents, and NIST says assurance cases for software were still under study.

Pick the system that already has one approved use and is most likely to get a second. Have its steward assemble the system part and start the register of uses, have the first owner write the use part and end it with the covers line, and name a reviewer from outside the team. When the next team asks, hand over the pack and ask that team's owner to answer the four questions for the new use. If the system has no approval for its first use yet, begin with "The Demo-to-Production Gap."
inside: Why a second team's request starts four new questions about the same system
An evidence pack in two parts, what each part holds, and who keeps it
Five triggers for testing again, the objections, and what no source tests
sourcesHtml: Gabriel Morgan Asaftei, Roger Roberts, Abby Sticha, and Cécile Prinsen, "State of AI trust in 2026: Shifting to the agentic era," McKinsey & Company, March 25, 2026 — McKinsey's 2026 AI Trust Maturity Survey, of about 500 organizations from December 2025 to January 2026, found nearly two-thirds of respondents naming security and risk concerns as the top barrier to fully scaling agentic AI. Organizations with clear ownership for responsible AI averaged 2.6 on its four-level maturity scale against 1.8 for those without a clearly accountable function. Both are survey results and an association, not causes.

Deloitte, "The State of AI in the Enterprise," 2026 AI report, Deloitte AI Institute — Deloitte's survey of 3,235 senior leaders, fielded August to September 2025, found that only one in five companies has a mature model for governance of autonomous AI agents. It reports leader answers, not the causes of stalled pilots.

Thomas Rhodes, Frederick Boland, Elizabeth Fong, and Michael Kass, "Software Assurance Using Structured Assurance Case Models," NIST Interagency Report 7608, National Institute of Standards and Technology, May 2009 — NIST's 2009 report describes a structured assurance case, a documented body of evidence for claims about a system in a given application and environment. It covers software, not AI, calls the method an active topic of research, and names further work on how much evidence is enough and on maintaining and revising cases.

Matthew Arnold, Rachel K. E. Bellamy, Michael Hind, Stephanie Houde, Sameep Mehta, Aleksandra Mojsilović, Ravi Nair, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Darrell Reimer, Alexandra Olteanu, David Piorkowski, Jason Tsay, and Kush R. It is a proposal with example answers for two fictional services, not a study of adoption, and a supplier writes it before it knows a given buyer's use.

It suggests documenting a system's knowledge limits, defining who reviews periodically, and re-evaluating risk when a model is adapted to a new domain.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — The NIST AI Risk Management Framework Core organizes AI risk work into govern, map, measure, and manage and describes it as continuous and iterative. It is voluntary and is not a checklist.

entries.title: The write-up you skipped never gets blamed
entries.summary: When a meeting ends and nobody writes down what was decided, the next team has to stop and ask or start and guess. The hour you saved comes back in their queue, logged as a clarification, a redesign, or a reopened decision. What it never gets logged as is the write-up nobody did.
entries.metaDescription: When nobody writes down what was decided, the next team stops and asks or starts and guesses. Five things to record before a cross-team handoff.
entries.operatingMove: Before you hand work to another team, write down what you decided, why, what you agreed to bend, who does what next, and when to revisit it. Then let them say whether the handoff is done.
entries.preview: The schedule is tight, so someone offers a sensible trade: start the handoff now, write up the decision later. Everyone in the meeting already knows what happened — but the next team was not in the room, so they stop and ask or start and guess. Either way the time comes back, and it comes back labeled as delivery trouble. The cost lands there under another name, which is why nobody traces it back to the meeting. Five things in the record close it, and the next team is the one who says whether they are there.
inside: Why the delay gets logged as a clarification or a redesign instead of the write-up nobody did
The five things the next team needs, and why they are the right judge of whether the record works
Who keeps the record accurate after the handoff, and what should bring it back up
sourcesHtml: Leopold Müller, Joshua Holstein, Sarah Bause, Gerhard Satzger, and Niklas Kühl, "Data Quality Challenges in Retrieval-Augmented Generation," arXiv:2510.00552, submitted October 1, 2025; accepted for ICIS 2025 — data-quality problems that start at the source carry through retrieval into the generated answer.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 2024 — NIST lists data provenance and data quality among the system details organizations should document, and suggests verifying that retrieval data is grounded.

International Organization for Standardization, "ISO 30401:2018 — Knowledge management systems — Requirements," November 2018 — ISO 30401 frames knowledge management as a system that is established, implemented, maintained, reviewed, and improved.

National Aeronautics and Space Administration, "Knowledge Management," APPEL Knowledge Services, updated June 12, 2026 — NASA's knowledge-management practice emphasizes continuity through capture, storage, reuse, and sharing.

Maria Olívia Ferreira Pereira, Helena de Fátima Nunes Silva, and José Simão de Paula Pinto, "A Memória organizacional nos processos de gestão do conhecimento: um estudo na Universidade Federal do Paraná," Informação & Informação 21, no. 1 (2016): 348–374 — organizational-memory research examines how knowledge is identified, recorded, used, and reused.
entries.bodyHtml:
Your steering group approved a change. The next team is ready to start. The schedule is already slipping, so someone makes a sensible-sounding offer: begin the handoff now, write up the decision later. It sounds fine, because everyone in the meeting already knows what happened. The next team does not.

They need to know what changed, why it changed, what you agreed to bend, and who is allowed to change it again. Without that, the person picking up the work has two choices: stop and ask, or start and guess. Both put more pressure on the schedule you were trying to protect.

So does starting sooner actually save time, once the decision has to cross into someone else's work? The answer shows up in what happens after the meeting.

Where the time actually goes

Writing it up is easy to skip because the cost is visible and immediate — an hour, right now, while the schedule slips. Starting the handoff is immediate too. The write-up looks like a separate job you can do any time.

Consider what can follow. A product team gets the scope change and comes back asking why. Operations designs the standard path and then finds out an exception was already agreed. A new manager reopens a settled decision because nobody wrote down what would have to change for it to be revisited.

Each of those can get logged as something else — a clarification, a redesign, a reopened decision. In this paper's reading, the choice to skip the write-up then does not appear in the account of the delay, so nothing in the record points back to it and the cause goes unfixed.

Let the next team decide when it is done

Records matter most at the seams — a decision moving from a steering group to delivery, a design moving between functions, a program moving into operations, one owner handing off to the next. This is where knowledge has to move from the people who have it to people who do not, and survive in a form those people can use.

Length and polish prove nothing. Hand the record to the person receiving the work and ask them to trace the action they are supposed to take back to the decision, the reason behind it, where it stops applying, and who can change it. If they have to come back to you for another meeting, that gap is what the handoff is still missing.

A record that passes does four jobs. It lets the next team act. It keeps the decision and the reasoning together. It stays useful after people leave. It also gives a person, or an AI system, something reliable to look up later. All four depend on the record working without its author standing next to it.

AI cannot tell you what the page left out

A retrieval system, the kind of tool that looks up stored pages to answer questions, can only find what the page actually contains. A missing reason, a missing exception, a missing owner, a missing date — none of that can be recovered from a page that never captured it. Research on retrieval systems finds that problems starting at the source carry through to the answer, and NIST lists where data came from and how good it is among the things organizations should write down. Neither tells a retrieval system who keeps the page current. Only the page can do that.

A colleague who hits an incomplete page knows who to call. A retrieval system sees the page, whatever is attached to it, and nothing else. A better model cannot supply context that was never written down — though bad documentation is only one of the things that can make an AI answer wrong.

Give the next team five things

At the next handoff that matters, require a short record with a name on it that answers five questions. What did we decide, and what is it meant to achieve? Why did we pick it? What did we agree to bend or leave open, and what cannot change? What happens next, and who owns it? What date or event should bring this back up?

The person who made the decision stays responsible for the content even if someone else writes the words. They confirm the reasoning, the limits, and when to revisit. The person receiving it confirms they can actually use it.

Ownership does not end at acceptance. A record people depend on turns dangerous when circumstances change underneath it, so someone has to be able to fix it, retire it, or flag the part where someone now has to decide for themselves. For retrieval tools, "AI Knowledge Bases Need Owners and Current Sources" covers this.

Back to the handoff you were about to rush. If the record passes the next team's test, they can start without guessing, and someone is on the hook for keeping it accurate. If it fails, you know exactly what to do — fill in what is missing before you hand it over. The schedule will still be urgent. What changes is when you call it done: not when the meeting ends, but when the person receiving the work can use what you wrote.

entries.title: Compare AI proposals on the work they change, not the demo
entries.summary: A portfolio review can face several AI proposals for the same people and budget, each backed by different evidence. The paper recommends one page for each, answering the same six questions, so the review can compare them side by side.
entries.metaDescription: Ask each AI proposal for the same one-page brief, then compare them side by side. A missing answer holds a proposal until it is supplied.
entries.operatingMove: Before the next review, ask the business owner of each AI proposal for the one-page brief. The analyst marks each answer as given or missing, and the chair decides each proposal's outcome and writes one line saying why.
entries.preview: In this paper's reading, a demo, a usage count, and a local time saving answer different questions, so none ranks one proposal against another. This field note describes the one page each proposal fills in, who writes and checks it, how the review compares the pages, and what a missing answer means. It also states the objections and what no source tests.
inside: What a demo, a usage count, and a local saving each show
The six questions on the one-page brief, and who writes it
How the review compares briefs and treats a missing answer
entries.bodyHtml:
You chair the portfolio review that decides which AI proposals receive scarce capacity: the people and budget that cannot cover every request. One team brings a working assistant. Another has a vendor demo. A third shows time saved on drafting and analysis. All three can produce something. None has shown which work should change, what result would matter, or why AI is the right investment.

This paper recommends that the review ask for the same one-page opportunity brief for every proposal and compare the proposals on the briefs, not on the demos. The business owner, the leader accountable for the results of the work the proposal would change, writes the brief. It answers six questions: what work or decision should change, what is happening there now, how value could appear, what evidence would earn the next step, who owns the result and what AI may decide, and what else could solve the problem. The next step is a small funded test with a result stated in advance. The brief does not produce a score. Its first job is to show which proposals can be compared yet, because a proposal with a missing answer cannot be ranked against one without.

A field study of 5,179 customer-support agents at one company found a 14 percent average productivity gain from an AI assistant, with the largest gains for novice workers. It shows that a tool can help one defined workflow. It does not show which work a company should choose to change, or that the workflow deserves capacity ahead of another team's proposal. In McKinsey's 2025 survey, 88 percent of respondents said their organizations regularly use AI in at least one function, and 39 percent attributed any level of earnings impact to AI at the enterprise level; most of those said less than 5 percent. Gartner reports that at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept, and says projects without a clear way to rank use cases or measure success lack measurable business value.

This paper's reading is that a demo, a usage count, and a local time saving answer different questions about a tool or a task, so they do not rank proposals against each other. No source tests that reading.

The portfolio analyst lays the briefs side by side and marks each answer as given or missing. A reviewer outside the proposing teams checks each baseline, the measurement of the problem today, and each evidence test, the result that would justify more investment. The review chair then decides, with no formula, because a score would hide the judgment of weighing delay against errors, cost, and risk, and writes one line of reasoning for each decision. A weak answer counts against a proposal. A missing answer means the proposal cannot be compared yet, so it is held with the missing answers named and receives no scarce capacity until they are supplied. Each proposal ends in one of four outcomes: fund the next step, hold it with the missing answers named, combine it with other work, or stop it.

A brief can slow exploration, so a low-cost trial by one team needs none. A business case may already answer the six questions, and then no second document is needed. A polished page or a hopeful baseline can win, so a reviewer outside the proposing teams checks the baseline. With no formula, the chair's discretion is limited only by the written reason for each decision. The estimates in a brief are guesses, which the brief makes checkable. No source tests the brief.

Before the next portfolio review, ask the business owner of each AI proposal to write the one-page brief, and ask that no brief name a tool before it names the work. The analyst marks the gaps before the meeting. The chair then decides each proposal's outcome and writes one line saying why. Expect missing answers the first time. The list of them is the first result.
sourcesHtml: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey R. Raymond, "Generative AI at Work," NBER Working Paper 31161, April 2023; revised November 2023; published in The Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), 2025, 889-942 — a field study of 5,179 customer-support agents at one company found a 14 percent average productivity gain from an AI assistant, 34 percent for novice and low-skilled workers and minimal for experienced workers. It measures one tool, one workflow, and one company.

Alex Singla, Alexander Sukharevsky, Bryce Hall, Lareina Yee, Michael Chui, and Tara Balakrishnan, "The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation," McKinsey & Company, November 5, 2025 — McKinsey's survey of 1,993 respondents reports that 88 percent regularly use AI in at least one function and that 39 percent attribute any level of earnings impact to AI at the enterprise level, most of them under 5 percent. These are respondents' own reports, so the survey cannot show cause.

Arun Chandrasekaran, "Why 50% of GenAI Projects Fail - And How to Beat the Odds," Gartner, January 26, 2026 — Gartner reports that at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, names lack of business value as the first failure point, and says projects without a clear way to rank use cases or measure success lack measurable value. The article says Gartner analyzed hundreds of implementations and shows no method.

James Ryseff, Brandon F. De Bruhl, and Sydne J. Newberry, "The Root Causes of Failure for Artificial Intelligence Projects and How They Can Succeed: Avoiding the Anti-Patterns of AI," RAND Corporation, 2024 — RAND interviewed 65 experienced data scientists and engineers, who most often named misunderstanding or miscommunication about a project's purpose as the reason AI projects failed. Most interviewees were engineers, so the results may be skewed toward identifying leadership failures. These are interviews, not a count of projects.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — NIST's framework asks organizations to define who is responsible when people and AI work together and who oversees the AI, and to document how human oversight works. It is voluntary and does not prescribe this paper's brief.

Johannes-Tobias Lorenz, Joshan Cherian Abraham, Robert Levin, and Douglas Ziman, "From promise to impact: How companies can measure—and realize—the full value of AI," McKinsey & Company, April 24, 2026 — McKinsey separates five levels of measurement for AI value: technical performance, user adoption, operating results, strategic outcomes, and financial impact. It is a consultancy's approach, not a tested standard.

entries.title: Benefits realization is where transformations quietly fail
entries.summary: A program can reach go-live with every delivery control green and still never be checked for the value it was funded to produce. The controls that run a program can end at go-live, and the value arrives afterward. A missed benefit can then go unseen. The fix is to settle at approval who answers for the value, how it will be measured, and when it will be reviewed.
entries.metaDescription: A program can ship and never be checked for its value. Settle an owner, a measure, and a review date at approval.
entries.operatingMove: At the next approval, add one page. It names the benefit owner, the measure and its baseline, the review date, and the decisions the review can take. Then check the largest program that went live in the past year for the same four things.
entries.preview: A program can be delivered on every control and still go unchecked for value. This paper explains why delivery governance can end before the benefit is due. It sets out five things to settle at approval. They are a benefit owner outside the delivery team, a measure of the result, a baseline, a benefit review with a decision attached, and a record for the next business case. It also covers how to separate the program's effect from other change, when to review, what it costs, and where the evidence is limited.
inside: Why delivery governance can end before the benefit is due, and what that leaves unchecked
Five things to settle at approval: owner, measure, baseline, review date, and record
How to separate the program's effect from other change, when to review, and what it costs
sourcesHtml: Project Management Institute, "Pulse of the Profession 2018: Success in Disruptive Times," 2018 — PMI's 2018 survey of project practitioners, executives, and directors of project management offices reports that one organization in three has high benefits realization maturity, which is a self-report. It names managing projects on time, scope, and budget without tracking strategic goals as a challenge many companies face.

U.S. General Accounting Office (now Government Accountability Office), Information Technology Investment Management: A Framework for Assessing and Improving Process Maturity, GAO-04-394G, March 2004 — GAO's 2004 guide to managing federal technology investments describes a review after launch that compares actual results with estimates, with a general guideline of 6 to 18 months adjusted for when the benefits are expected. It is federal guidance, not an outcome study.

Michael Bloch, Sven Blumberg, and Jürgen Laartz, "Delivering large-scale IT projects on time, on budget, and on value," McKinsey & Company (with the University of Oxford), October 1, 2012 — McKinsey and the University of Oxford compared predicted and actual results for more than 5,400 IT projects. In a 2012 article, large ones averaged 45 percent over budget, 7 percent over time, and 56 percent less value than predicted. The study covers large IT projects, not transformations in general.

Patrick Forth, Tom Reichert, Romain de Laubier, and Saibal Chakraborty, "Flipping the Odds of Digital Transformation Success," Boston Consulting Group, October 29, 2020 — BCG combined 825 executives' ratings of their own digital transformations with 70 client programs. About 30 percent met target value with lasting change. The score is self-rated and includes timing, and the report links outcome tracking to winning programs without testing cause.

U.S. Government Accountability Office, Designing Evaluations: 2012 Revision, GAO-12-208G, January 2012 — GAO's guide to designing evaluations explains that an observed outcome mixes a program's effect with outside factors, and that comparison groups help separate them. It was written for public programs.

Bent Flyvbjerg, "Quality Control and Due Diligence in Project Management: Getting Decisions Right by Taking the Outside View," International Journal of Project Management, 2013 — Flyvbjerg reports that front-end estimates of costs and benefits often differ significantly from actual results, drawing mostly on large transport projects, and proposes checking a forecast against the track record of similar ones.
entries.bodyHtml:
A program can go live with every delivery control green and still never be checked for the value it was funded to produce. Delivery governance, meaning the schedule, budget, and scope controls that run a program, can end at go-live, and the value arrives afterward. The argument is narrow. Delivery also fails, and no source reviewed here shows which stage most transformations fail at. The point is that after go-live nothing may compare the results with the business case, so a missed benefit can go unseen, and the next program is approved on the same unchecked kind of business case. Benefits realization, the work of confirming that a program produced its expected result, is not a new idea. The Project Management Institute (PMI) tracks it as a maturity measure, and U.S. federal technology guidance describes how to review it. PMI's 2018 survey found one organization in three reporting high maturity at it, which is a self-report.

The fix is to settle five things at approval, before anyone is reassigned. A benefit owner, an operating leader outside the delivery team, answers for the value after go-live. A measure tracks the result the program was funded to change, such as fewer repeat contacts and not logins. A baseline, the starting reading of that measure, is taken before the work starts. A benefit review is booked for a date after launch with a decision attached: accept the benefit, invest more, change the approach, or stop. Each result then goes into a record the next business case can be set beside. The paper adds ways to separate the program's effect from other change, to time the review, and to handle a program that has no baseline, and it says what owning the benefit costs.

The paper also says where it is weaker. Many changes affect the same result, so what a program can credit itself with is a contribution, not a precise share. Measuring costs money. The PMI figure is self-reported, and none of the sources tested whether booking a review at approval raises the value a program realizes. The five-thing design, and the requirement that the owner sit outside the delivery team, are the paper's own.

entries.title: Automate, build, buy, hire, or wait
entries.summary: In this paper's observation, an AI request often arrives with its response already chosen: buy this, build that. Gartner reports that at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025. The paper recommends comparing five responses first, with proof set by how hard each is to undo. A wait gets a record of what brings the request back, who watches for it, and when to look again. The rule is the paper's own design, and no source tests it.
entries.metaDescription: Compare automating, building, buying, hiring or training, and waiting for an AI request. Set the proof by how hard each is to undo, and give a wait a trigger.
entries.operatingMove: Take one AI request whose problem has been named. Put the five responses on one page, remove any that fail the screen, and set the proof by how hard each is to undo. If the result is to wait, write what brings the request back, who watches for it, the review date, and what the delay costs.
entries.preview: This paper puts five responses to an AI request on one page: automate, build, buy, hire or train, and wait. It gives a three-step rule for choosing, three levels of proof set by how hard a response is to undo, and a wait record with what brings the request back, an owner, a review date, and the cost of delay. It works one example through the rule and states the objections: added process, waiting that drifts, and a rule no source tests.
inside: A three-step rule for choosing among five responses to an AI request
How hard a response is to undo sets how much proof it needs
How to run a wait: what brings it back, who watches, when to look again
sourcesHtml: Gartner, "Gartner Predicts 30% of Generative AI Projects Will Be Abandoned After Proof of Concept By End of 2025," July 29, 2024 — Gartner's July 2024 release forecasts that at least 30 percent of generative AI projects will be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025. It also describes expanding an investment that meets expectations, or exploring alternatives if it falls short. It is a forecast and shows no method.

Arun Chandrasekaran, "Why 50% of GenAI Projects Fail - And How to Beat the Odds," Gartner, January 26, 2026 — Gartner reports that at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, citing poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, or unclear business value. The page says Gartner analyzed hundreds of implementations and shows no method.

James Ryseff, Brandon F. De Bruhl, and Sydne J. Newberry, "The Root Causes of Failure for Artificial Intelligence Projects and How They Can Succeed: Avoiding the Anti-Patterns of AI," RAND Corporation, 2024 — RAND interviewed 65 experienced data scientists and engineers about failed AI projects and names five root causes, including missing data, and describes leaders demanding AI for problems that simple rules could solve. Most interviewees were engineers, not executives, and the interviews are not a count of projects.

Gartner, "Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027," June 25, 2025 — Gartner says many vendors relabel existing assistants, chatbots, and automation tools as agentic AI, and estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real. The estimate covers agentic AI vendors only and shows no method.

Robert S. Pindyck, “Irreversibility, Uncertainty, and Investment,” Journal of Economic Literature 29(3), 1991, 1110–1148; NBER Working Paper 3307, 1990 — Pindyck's economic analysis of investment under uncertainty: an irreversible investment gives up the chance to wait for new information, which is a cost, and delay has its own cost. It is theory about business investment in general, not a study of AI.

NIST, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — NIST's framework lists procedures for decommissioning AI systems and for superseding, disengaging, or deactivating one whose results are inconsistent with its intended use. It is voluntary and does not set how much proof a purchase needs.

Johannes-Tobias Lorenz, Joshan Cherian Abraham, Robert Levin, and Douglas Ziman, "From promise to impact: How companies can measure and realize the full value of AI," McKinsey & Company, April 24, 2026 — McKinsey says many organizations deploy AI in ways that are more visible than valuable, and sets out an approach to measuring AI value. It is a consultancy's view, not a measured rate.
entries.bodyHtml:
A steering group, the people who decide where a company's money and staff go, receives an AI request that has already picked its response. A team wants to buy a drafting assistant, build an agent, or automate a report, and the review is asked to say yes or no. That is this paper's observation of how requests are often framed. No source counts how often.

Gartner reported in January 2026 that at least half of generative AI projects were abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, citing poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs, and unclear business value. In July 2024 it had forecast 30 percent, citing the same four causes. The article shows no method, so neither figure says how often a different choice would have helped. RAND's interviews with 65 data scientists and engineers also name missing data among five leading causes of failed AI projects.

Once the recurring work and the step that most limits it are named, compare five responses before funding any of them: automate the work, build a capability, buy a tool, hire or train people, or wait. Ask the same six questions of each. Does it relieve the limiting step? Is what it needs in place? What does it cost over the period the organization is committed to it? What can go wrong? Can the organization carry it? How hard is it to undo?

Drop any response that cannot relieve the limiting step. Send one that needs something not yet in place to wait, with the missing item as its trigger. Replace one that is hard to undo and lacks the proof its level calls for with a smaller version that is easy to undo. Rank the rest by how much each relieves against its total cost for each year of commitment. When two are close, the one that is easier to undo wins. The business owner, the leader accountable for the work's results, decides, and a portfolio analyst keeps all five on one page. The rule and the planning estimates of its cost are the paper's own design, and no source tests them.

Pindyck's analysis of investment under uncertainty shows that an irreversible choice gives up the chance to wait for new information, and that the lost chance is a cost. The paper turns that idea into three levels. A response that is easy to undo needs the baseline, a stated reason, and a review date. One that is costly to undo needs a small test in real work. One that is practically permanent, such as a multi-year contract, a custom build, or removed roles, needs the full operating case and a written way out, and the steering group decides.

A wait is a response with its own record: a trigger, an owner, a review date, and a stated cost of delay. A trigger is a named event or measurement that brings the request back for a decision. A wait with no trigger or no owner counts as a stop.

The comparison can add process to every idea, so it scales with how hard a response is to undo. Waiting can drift, so the review date forces a decision. Five ways the choice goes wrong are automation theater, prestige building, procurement substitution, headcount avoidance, and passive waiting, and the paper says which part of the rule catches each. Pindyck's analysis is theory about business investment in general, and no source compares building with buying or hiring.

Before the next steering meeting, take one AI request whose problem has been named. Have a portfolio analyst write the five responses on one page, one line each, answering the same six questions. The business owner marks each response's level, applies the screen, ranks what remains, settles any tie toward the response that is easier to undo, and states the proof the chosen response must show before it expands. If the choice is to wait, the page carries the trigger, the wait's owner, the review date, and what the delay costs.

entries.title: AI usage belongs in workflow governance, not blank-check access
entries.summary: Govern AI access where the work happens, and match the controls to what is at stake in that particular workflow.
entries.operatingMove: Set AI permissions at the workflow level. Match the access, the review, and the evidence you require to the data involved, what happens if the output is wrong, and how easily you can recover.
entries.preview: A blanket access policy treats every AI use as if the data, the consequences, and the recovery path were the same. This paper moves the decision into the workflow, where the differences are visible. It shows how to sort uses by what is at stake, and how to define what is allowed and what must be recorded. Review and escalation get assigned without pushing low-risk work through the same controls as decisions that matter.
inside: Why one AI account can carry two completely different levels of risk
Six controls that make a workflow governable, and when to reach for stronger ones
How to start with a single usage record instead of a blanket policy
sourcesHtml: Gabriel Morgan Asaftei, Roger Roberts, Abby Sticha, and Cécile Prinsen, "State of AI trust in 2026: Shifting to the agentic era," McKinsey & Company, March 25, 2026 — McKinsey's analysis extends the risk from wrong statements to wrong actions, tool misuse, and operation beyond guardrails.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," AI RMF 1.0, 2023 — NIST's AI Risk Management Framework organizes risk work through govern, map, measure, and manage, and treats context of use as material.

International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission, "ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system," 2023 — ISO/IEC 42001 sets requirements for an AI management system in organizations that provide or use AI.

Chloe Autio, Reva Schwartz, Jesse Dunietz, Shomik Jain, Martin Stanley, Elham Tabassi, Patrick Hall, and Kamie Roberts, "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile," NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024 — NIST's Generative AI Profile calls for continuous monitoring, structured feedback, and incident response across the lifecycle.

Taryn Plumb, "Roughly half of employees are using unsanctioned AI tools, and enterprise leaders are major culprits," CIO, January 29, 2026 — A survey commissioned by BlackFog found 49 percent of employees using AI tools their employer had not sanctioned; it shows how common the use is, not why.
entries.bodyHtml:
One AI account can carry two different risks

Your organization has approved an AI tool and wants more people to use it. The access decision looks responsible: an approved vendor, sign-on controls, an acceptable-use policy, and licenses assigned to the right employees.

Now follow two uses of the same account. One employee asks the tool to draft an internal meeting note. Another uses it in work that affects a customer. An agent might even trigger a later action. The license record looks the same in both cases. It cannot reveal the harm an error could cause or how much authority the AI had. It also leaves the review point and stop authority unknown.

That leaves the CIO or AI-governance leader with a bad choice. Heavy approval on every low-stakes use can drive people around the approved path. Blank-check access, meaning light controls on every use, lets high-impact work proceed without evidence, limits, escalation, or ownership.

Build the missing record around consequence

Account approval opens the capability; a separate workflow record must name the work AI may perform, the decision or action it can influence, the evidence it must leave, and the owner who can stop it. That record lets the organization keep a low-stakes drafting path light. Work that shapes a high-impact decision or performs an external action gets stronger controls.

Use six controls for each high-impact workflow. Scope access to the approved work. Monitor actual use. Set limits on volume, rate, or autonomy. Retain evidence and logs. Name the review path, escalation path, and owner. Set a date to review how it is used.

The six controls stay the same while their weight changes. Internal drafting may need an approved tool, light monitoring, and clear information limits. Customer-impacting decisions need evidence, review, escalation, and ownership. AI tools that act also need limits on permitted actions and autonomy. Those limits contain a bad setup before it travels.

Monitoring is the practical starting point. It shows whether the controls work and whether dependence has changed. A customer-impacting use might track AI-triggered actions, human overrides, limit breaches, and escalations. Those signals show when dependence or autonomy has raised the stakes.

Usage limits contain operational harm. The owner can bound volume, rate, permitted actions, or autonomy. A bad setup can then stop before it reaches more systems or people. Cost may fall too, but low cost does not make the authority safe.

The approved route also has to meet a real workflow need and remain easy to find. If the path is impractical, people may choose tools outside it. Monitoring can expose that unmet demand. A high-impact use may still need to be blocked. Leaders can also correct the approved route for valid work.

Start with one usage-control record

Before expanding AI into a high-impact workflow, require one short record. Name the workflow, its owner, and the work AI may perform. List the signals to monitor and the limits on volume, rate, or autonomy. State what evidence to retain. Add the human review and escalation path, then set the next review date.

This does not require a heavy approval process around every user. Low-stakes work can be documented lightly. High-impact work gets the full control set before dependence or autonomy increases. As evidence changes, the owner can expand, narrow, redesign, or stop the use.

The sources support context-based governance, ongoing monitoring, guardrails, and human responsibility. They do not set one universal threshold. They also do not prove that this exact record improves adoption. The CIO or AI-governance leader must still judge each workflow on the data involved, the harm an error could cause, and the ability to recover. Simplify a record that never changes a control decision.

The organization can still expand AI access. It now knows where that access enters real work, what the AI may do, how a mistake is contained, and who decides when the use changes.

entries.title: AI should make people better thinkers, not just faster producers
entries.summary: A polished AI answer can hide who formed the view, tested it, and owns the final decision. The evidence for a fix comes from students, so the paper proposes a one-quarter pilot.
entries.operatingMove: For high-judgment work, have people state their first view, key assumptions, and what would change their mind. Then let AI challenge it. Pilot it for one quarter in one function.
entries.preview: Answer-first AI can speed up work while hiding the judgment behind it. Student trials and a small developer experiment suggest that how AI is used changes what people keep, but no large workplace trial has tested forming a view first. This field note sets out the position, how a reviewer scores the reasoning, five objections, and a one-quarter pilot.
inside: What the student trials and a small developer experiment show, and what no large workplace trial has tested
Why a human signature is not the same as skilled review, and how a reviewer scores the reasoning
Five objections, and how to pilot a three-step pre-mortem in one quarter of real work
sourcesHtml: Microsoft and LinkedIn, 2024 Work Trend Index Annual Report. Survey of 31,000 people, 31 markets, Feb–Mar 2024. The 78% figure for bringing your own AI tools includes any personal tool use supplementary to employer-provided tools and may overstate fully unsanctioned behavior. Only 39% of AI users had received AI training from their company — this survey reports widespread use of personal AI tools at work and limited company training among AI users.

Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakci, O., and Mariman, R. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning. PNAS, 122(26), e2422633122. Pre-registered RCT; ~1,000 students, 9th–11th grade; Turkey; IRB-approved. August 2025 correction updated one author's affiliation only; findings unchanged — this pre-registered student trial compared standard AI, a guarded tutor, and no AI.

Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., and Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning. Scientific Reports. RCT with crossover design; 233 enrolled, 194 eligible Harvard undergraduates; introductory physics; fall 2023. Effect size 0.73–1.3; p < 10⁻⁸. Critical limitations: selected population; two topics; introductory material; authors do not presume the result extends to complex synthesis and higher-order critical thinking — this student trial compared a custom AI tutor with active learning in two introductory physics topics.

Shen, J. H., and Tamkin, A. (2026). How AI Impacts Skill Formation. arXiv:2601.20245 (v2, February 2026). Preprint, not peer reviewed; the authors are affiliated with Anthropic. Randomized experiment; 52 software developers (26 with an AI assistant, 26 without), recruited through a crowd-work platform, most professional or freelance, learning a Python library in about one hour. AI group scored 4.15 points lower on a 27-point quiz (a 17 percent difference; d = 0.738, p = 0.01); no statistically significant speed-up. The higher-scoring interaction patterns were identified afterward and were not randomized — this randomized preprint of 52 developers learning a new library found lower quiz scores with an AI assistant; the interaction-pattern comparison was not randomized.

Dell'Acqua, F., et al. (2026). Navigating the jagged technological frontier. Organization Science, 37(2), 403–423; first circulated as HBS Working Paper No. 24-013 (2023). Pre-registered; n=758 BCG consultants. "Blindly adopt" wording is from the working paper; its retainment measure (copying AI output) was associated with better in-frontier performance. BCG co-designed a study finding BCG consultants perform better with AI; pre-registration and multi-institutional authorship partially mitigate this — this field experiment compared consultant performance on tasks inside and outside the model's tested range.

Groot, T., and Valdenegro-Toro, M. (2024). Overconfidence is Key: Verbalized Uncertainty Evaluation in Large Language and Vision-Language Models. Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Trustworthy Natural Language Processing (TrustNLP 2024), ACL, pp. 145-171. Tested GPT-4, GPT-3.5, LLaMA 2 and PaLM 2 (and two vision-language models); finds high calibration error and models "overconfident most of the time." Models of 2023 — this workshop paper tested four 2023 language models and found them overconfident most of the time.

Khanna, M., Wang, Z., Wei, L., and Xue, L. (2025). When Medical AI Explanations Help and When They Harm. arXiv:2512.08424 (v1, unreviewed preprint). n=257 medical students; 3,855 diagnostic decisions. Explanations raise accuracy when the AI is right (about 73 percent of cases) and lower it when wrong (about 27 percent); high-competence participants with appropriate uncertainty lose the most when the AI errs (-12.4 percentage points, p < 0.01), overconfident novices gain (+9.9 net) — this preprint of 257 medical students found that AI explanations helped when the advice was right and hurt when it was wrong; it is not a study of expert work.

Lee, H-P., et al. (2025). The impact of generative AI on critical thinking. CHI '25, Yokohama. Microsoft Research. "Task stewardship" is the authors' own framing. Limitations: self-report; cross-sectional; critical thinking not objectively measured; causality not established — this CHI study links confidence in AI with lower self-reported critical-thinking effort; it does not establish causation.

Gerlich, M. (2025). AI tools in society: Impacts on cognitive offloading and the future of critical thinking. Societies, 15(1), 6. n=666. Correlational; recommends balanced AI integration, which the study did not test. No objective performance measures — this correlational study links frequent AI use, cognitive offloading, and critical-thinking scores; it did not test a better way to use it.

Autor, D., and Thompson, N. (2025). Expertise. NBER Working Paper 33941. The inference that AI is specifically automating the non-expert tasks of knowledge work is the author's application of their analysis; Autor and Thompson do not make this specific claim about generative AI — this labor-economics paper explains how automation of expert and less-skilled tasks can affect employment and wages; the AI application is the author's inference.

Klein, G. (2007). Performing a project premortem. Harvard Business Review, 85(9), 18–19. Tested in: Veinott, E. S., Klein, G., and Wiggins, S. (2010). Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence. ISCRAM, Seattle (lab study, college students, hypothetical outbreak plan; read through secondary descriptions, not the original proceedings). The adaptation here — individual cognitive priming before AI engagement — extends Klein's team-based technique and has not been independently validated in that specific form — Klein's team pre-mortem and a lab study with college students inform the paper's untested individual adaptation.

Ma, S., et al. (2024). "Are you really sure?" CHI '24, Honolulu. Three studies; "Think the Opposite" was tested in Study 2 without AI assistance, and Study 3 found that confidence calibration reduced under-reliance on AI but not over-reliance. The intervention is similar to the pre-mortem prompt protocol and was developed independently. Limitation: income-prediction task in a lab setting — these studies tested confidence calibration and a think-the-opposite prompt, with mixed effects on how far people followed the AI.
entries.bodyHtml:
Suppose your team now turns in AI-assisted work faster. One recommendation reads well and reaches review early. A leader asks which assumptions carry the decision and what evidence would overturn it, and no one can answer without opening the chat again. The tool did more than help write the analysis. It supplied the first view, the challenge, and the wording of the decision.

This paper's position is that, for work that depends on judgment, people should form and defend a view before AI answers. The evidence is thinner than the position. The strongest results come from students, and no large workplace trial has tested the idea on experienced people doing their own expert work. So the position is the paper's inference, not a finding, and the paper ends with a one-quarter pilot.

The same model can support a different habit

Two randomized trials show why the interaction matters. Bastani and colleagues studied nearly 1,000 high-school students. Students with a standard AI tool later scored 17 percent below a no-AI group on an exam without the tool. A guarded version of the same model led students through hints and largely avoided that loss. Kestin and colleagues tested a custom AI tutor in introductory physics at Harvard. The AI group had more than twice the median learning gain of a class using active learning, in two topics over two weeks.

The trials used different students, subjects, and designs. Neither tested the first-view step described below or experienced workers, so neither proves a workplace will get the same result. The closest test with working adults is a randomized experiment with 52 software developers learning a new library. Those who used an AI assistant scored 17 percent lower on a quiz about it. Developers who asked for explanations tended to score higher than those who handed over the coding, but they chose their own approach, so that part was not randomized. It was one task, about an hour of work, and a preprint.

A review step needs skill and ownership

The usual phrase, “human in the loop,” is too weak on its own. It does not say whether the person can spot a poor assumption, check the evidence, or reject the answer. It also does not say who makes the final decision. A late signature is not the same as review.

Workplace evidence makes that distinction useful. In a field experiment with 758 consultants, AI users did better on tasks inside the model's tested range. On one task outside that range, they were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer. People whose results fell tended to accept the AI output and question it less. In a study of medical students, a wrong AI explanation sounded as convincing as a right one.

Make people form a view before they ask

For high-judgment work, start with a short pre-mortem, adapted from Gary Klein's team technique of imagining a plan has failed. Before opening the tool, the worker states the answer they expect, names the assumptions that must be true, and says what evidence would change their mind. AI then challenges that first view. The worker checks the challenge and owns the conclusion.

A reviewer who knows the subject then reads the record and checks four things. Was the first view written before the tool answered? Are the assumptions specific enough to be wrong? Did the worker act on each challenge? Does the final decision name its owner and say what changed? The reviewer does not decide whether the conclusion is right. The reading takes about ten minutes, as a planning estimate. This scoring is the paper's design, and no study has tested it.

Support the habit in three places

Training should teach people to test assumptions and evidence, not just write prompts. IT and operations should give them a safe, usable tool and require stronger checks when the cost of error is high. Managers should ask what changed the person's view and who makes the decision. If any one of those pieces is missing, deadline pressure is likely to push the work back toward ask, receive, and paste.

Pilot it for one quarter, and expect objections

Choose one function where judgment already matters, such as strategy, risk, client advice, or product decisions, and where someone can read a record with knowledge of the subject. Name one executive owner. For one quarter, require the three-step pre-mortem on selected work. Compare speed, rework, errors, and review quality with the function's earlier quarter. That comparison can show cost and fit, not proof.

Expect objections, among them that the step slows the work, senior experts may reject it, and a written first view may anchor people. Plan for them: the owner and the most senior reviewers use the step first, the pilot tracks how often the final decision differs from the first view, and it stops if neither rework nor errors fall. Then decide whether to expand, change, or stop. AI should help people think better, not make their thinking disappear behind a polished response.

entries.title: The AI replacement boomerang is a governance failure
entries.summary: Cutting people because AI can do part of their work books a saving at once. Gartner (for customer service) and Forrester forecast that many such cuts will be abandoned or quietly reversed. This paper argues the cost returns when nobody first checks what the role carried.
entries.metaDescription: Gartner (customer service) and Forrester forecast that many AI cuts will be dropped or reversed. Check what the role carried first.
entries.operatingMove: Before booking the saving from an AI-driven cut, attach a one-page record. It answers five questions, from what the role carried beyond its task to what would show the cut was wrong. A missing answer holds the saving.
entries.preview: A pilot shows that an AI tool can do part of a team's work, and a cost review turns that into a headcount saving. Gartner (for customer service) and Forrester forecast that many such cuts will be abandoned or quietly reversed. This paper sets out what the forecasts show and do not show. It gives a one-page check and a way to find out what a role carried. It also says where the argument is weaker.

The one-page check, the warning signs to read against a baseline, and when full automation is right

Betsy Summers, "Predictions 2026: The Workforce Muddles Through Ambient Disruption," Forrester blog, November 12, 2025 — Forrester's Predictions 2026 blog post says it expects half of AI-attributed layoffs to be quietly reversed, with jobs returning offshore or at lower wages; it is a forecast, and the full report is open to clients only.

David Mallon, Brad Kreit, and Natasha Buckley, "Rethinking operating models for humans with agents," Deloitte Insights, April 2, 2026 — Deloitte's operating-models article reports that its State of AI in the Enterprise 2026 survey found 84 percent of companies had not redesigned jobs to fit AI; the figure measures redesign, not workforce cuts.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, "Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence," Stanford Digital Economy Lab, working paper, November 13, 2025 — The Stanford Digital Economy Lab study of ADP payroll data found a 16 percent relative employment decline for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, concentrated where AI use looks like automation; it classifies occupations from conversations with one AI assistant, not from employer decisions.

Alexander Sukharevsky, Alexis Krivkovich, Arne Gast, Arsen Storozhev, Dana Maor, Deepak Mahadevan, Lari Hämäläinen, and Sandra Durth, "The agentic organization: Contours of the next paradigm for the AI era," McKinsey & Company, September 26, 2025 — McKinsey argues that AI-first work is a redesign of end-to-end processes with people above the loop, and also says agents are replacing tasks historically handled by knowledge workers; it is a consulting argument, not a measured result.

Lisanne Bainbridge, "Ironies of Automation," Automatica 19(6), 1983, 775–779 — Bainbridge's 1983 paper argues that automating routine work erodes the practice that builds operator skill; her examples come from industrial plants.

National Institute of Standards and Technology, "AI Risk Management Framework Core," excerpt from Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), January 2023 — NIST's AI Risk Management Framework Core describes govern, map, measure, and manage as an ongoing cycle for AI risk; it is guidance, not evidence about workforce cuts.
entries.bodyHtml:
A cost review receives a proposal. A pilot showed that an AI tool can do a routine part of a team's work, so the proposal cuts the team and books the saving. Two analyst firms forecast that many plans like this will not hold. Gartner predicts that by 2027, half of the organizations that expected to significantly reduce their customer service workforce because of AI will abandon those plans. Forrester expects half of the layoffs attributed to AI to be quietly reversed. Those jobs would return offshore or at lower wages. These are forecasts, not counts. The same figures mean that about half of the plans and layoffs will hold.

Neither forecast measures why one company's cut fails and another's does not. The paper's inference is that cuts come back when the decision starts from what the tool can do. In that case nobody first checks what the role carried beyond the task, who will own the hard cases (the unusual ones a routine process cannot settle), or how junior staff will become senior ones. Stanford researchers found a 16 percent relative decline in employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations, compared with the least exposed. The declines were concentrated where AI use looked like automating work rather than helping a person do it. The study sorts occupations by how people use one AI assistant, not by what employers decided, so it cannot show who made the choice. Inside a single company, whether a deployment automates or augments is a design choice leaders can govern.

The proposed remedy is a redesign gate, a required check before anyone books the saving from an AI-driven headcount cut. The proposal's sponsor answers five questions on one page. They run from what the role carried to what would show the decision was wrong. A missing answer holds the saving. The paper also explains how to find out what a role carried and what that costs. It covers where the argument is weaker, including cases where full automation is the right answer. Keep the decision reversible until the warning signs have been read against a baseline taken before the cut.

entries.title: AI knowledge bases need owners and current sources
entries.summary: An AI answer can sound right while citing an old policy. Name who approves each source, when it must be checked again, and how readers can trace the answer back to it.
entries.metaDescription: Retrieval can find the right source and still be wrong when the business no longer accepts it. Source-entry ownership is what makes an AI answer reliable.
entries.operatingMove: Choose one area where a wrong answer would matter. Have a named owner approve its sources, then test real questions against those pages.
entries.preview: The AI found the policy page and used it correctly. The answer was still wrong because the page had been replaced. This field note shows how an owner, five source checks, and a trace from answer to approved page make that error easier to prevent and find.
entries.bodyHtml:
A sponsor tests an AI assistant before staff use it at work. It gives a clear answer and cites a policy page. Then the team finds out that the page was replaced six months ago. The assistant found the page and used it correctly. The answer was still wrong.

Staff may trust that answer because it sounds right. As more people use the tool, wrong answers can shape decisions before anyone finds the old page. A shared knowledge base needs an owner who can say which sources still apply.

Approve the source before AI uses it

A study of AI systems that retrieve documents before answering found many data problems in the sources and the process that loads them. The researchers interviewed practitioners; they did not measure how much each defect changes an answer. Their work shows why source quality deserves an early check.

Better search or a new model may help the tool find and explain a page. Neither can decide which of two conflicting policies the company accepts. A source owner must decide which policy applies before the page enters the trusted set.

Use five checks. Name the owner. Check quality. Set a date or event for review. Limit who may read or change the page. Mark it as under review, current, replaced, or removed. Reject a page while a key question has no answer or an important conflict remains.

Keep a path from each answer to its approved page. Record the owner, last check, reason for approval, and any replacement. This lets a reviewer see where an answer came from and whether its source still applies.

Start where a wrong answer matters

Choose one area where a wrong answer could change an approval, access decision, or customer promise. Approve its pages, then ask real questions and trace each answer back to a current source. Expand when the owner and reviewers can keep that link sound.

Source checks cannot make every AI answer correct. The assistant must still find and use the right page. The checks settle the business decisions the technology cannot make: which page counts, who may change it, and when it must be checked again.

Five checks before AI is allowed to use a page
How to trace an answer back to the approved source
